articles.title: Trick or Type Guard? Surviving `unknown` with is-kit 🎃
articles.description: Hoi hoi! 👋  I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who is scared of horror things 🙀  Happy Halloween!...
articles.body_html:
Hoi hoi! 👋

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who is scared of horror things 🙀

Happy Halloween! 🎃👻

Tonight, we're exploring a haunted TypeScript project.

There are zombies 🧟, ghosts 👻, mysterious pumpkins 🎃, and a terrifying vampire 🧛 waiting for us.

And they all have something to do with TypeScript types!

Our mission?

Survive the night without losing type safety! 😸

Let's go!

🧟 Chapter 1: The Unknown Living Dead

It's a dark and spooky night.

Suddenly, something crawls out of the grave! 🧟

const creature: unknown = JSON.parse('{"message":"BRAAAINS!"}');

Oh! An unknown creature!

Let's see what it wants.

console.log(creature.message);
// ❌ 'creature' is of type 'unknown'.

WHAT?! 🙀

TypeScript won't let us!

But why?

Well, because we don't actually know what creature is.

It might be a zombie.
It might be a ghost.
It might even be a cute little cat. 😸

unknown means we haven't verified the value yet.

Unlike any, TypeScript won't let us access arbitrary properties on an unknown value.

And that's actually a good thing!

Let's try something simpler.

import { isString } from "is-kit";

const voice: unknown = JSON.parse('"BRAAAINS!"');

if (isString(voice)) {
  console.log(voice.toUpperCase());
  // BRAAAINS!
}

YAY! 🎉

We survived our first encounter!

Of course, we could also use typeof voice === 'string' here.

For a single check, that's perfectly fine!

But what happens when our monsters become bigger and more complicated?

🎃 Chapter 2: The Big Pumpkin of Unknown

Look!

A GIGANTIC PUMPKIN! 🎃

And apparently, it's full of candy.

But nobody knows what's really inside.

const pumpkin: unknown = JSON.parse(`{
  "name": "Big Pumpkin",
  "candies": ["Chocolate", "Lollipop", "Cookie"],
  "spookyLevel": 99,
  "keeper": {
    "name": "cat",
    "friendly": true
  },
  "secret": "Meow!"
}`);

That's a pretty big object.

Can we just grab the candy?

console.log(pumpkin.candies);
// ❌ 'pumpkin' is of type 'unknown'.

Not again! 😿

We need to check what's inside before touching anything.

Fortunately, we have struct!

import {
  arrayOf,
  isBoolean,
  isNumber,
  isString,
  optionalKey,
  struct,
} from "is-kit";

const isPumpkin = struct({
  name: isString,
  candies: arrayOf(isString),
  spookyLevel: isNumber,
  keeper: struct({
    name: isString,
    friendly: isBoolean,
  }),
  secret: optionalKey(isString),
});

We composed several small guards into one big pumpkin guard.

  • isString checks strings.
  • isNumber checks finite numbers.
  • arrayOf(isString) checks an array of strings.
  • struct checks nested object shapes.
  • optionalKey allows a property to be missing.

Now, let's open the pumpkin!

import { safeParse } from "is-kit";

const result = safeParse(isPumpkin, pumpkin);

if (result.valid) {
  console.log(result.value.candies);
  // ['Chocolate', 'Lollipop', 'Cookie']

  console.log(result.value.keeper.name);
  // cat 😸
}

We found the candy!!! 🍬🎉

When validation succeeds, result.value has the type inferred from our guards.

And when validation fails?

const cursedPumpkin = {
  name: "Cursed Pumpkin",
  candies: "100 candies",
  spookyLevel: 99,
  keeper: {
    name: "cat",
    friendly: true,
  },
};

const result = safeParse(isPumpkin, cursedPumpkin);

console.log(result);
// { valid: false }

The candies were a string, not an array!

Our guard rejected the cursed pumpkin.

And here's the important part.

safeParse doesn't magically fix or convert invalid values.

It simply tells us whether the value passed our guard.

Also, struct allows extra properties by default. If you need to reject additional own enumerable string keys, you can use { exact: true }.

Nice and simple!

🍬 Chapter 3: Trick or Type Guard!

Ding dong! 🔔

TRICK OR TREAT!!! 😸

Someone hands us a mysterious gift.

function receiveGift(): unknown {
  return Math.random() > 0.5 ? "Chocolate" : { spiders: 100 };
}

const gift: unknown = receiveGift();

Wait.

Is it candy?
Or is it a box full of spiders?! 🕷️😱

We need a way to check!

And this time, we want to accept either a string or a number.

Let's combine our guards with or!

import { isNumber, isString, or } from "is-kit";

const isTreat = or(isString, isNumber);

function trickOrTreat(gift: unknown) {
  if (isTreat(gift)) {
    // gift: string | number
    return `🍬 Treat: ${gift}`;
  }

  return "👻 Trick!";
}

Now let's try it!

trickOrTreat("Chocolate");
// 🍬 Treat: Chocolate

trickOrTreat(100);
// 🍬 Treat: 100

trickOrTreat({ spiders: 100 });
// 👻 Trick!

YAY!!! 🍬

No spiders for us today!

This is one of my favorite things about is-kit.

We don't need to write one giant validator.

We can build small guards, combine them, and reuse them wherever we need.

Small guards. Simple composition. Useful TypeScript narrowing.

That's the idea!

But wait,
Something is coming.
Something TERRIFYING.

🧛 Final Boss: The Vampire Called any

Suddenly, the lights go out.

The door opens.

A mysterious figure appears in the darkness.

It's... COUNT ANY!!! 🧛💀

The most terrifying vampire in our TypeScript project! And he has a very dangerous power.

He can make TypeScript stop checking our operations!

const visitor: unknown = JSON.parse('{"name":666}');

A mysterious visitor has arrived.

Normally, TypeScript protects us from accessing properties before we verify them.

But Count Any has a trick.

THE CURSE OF as any! 🧛

const vampire = visitor as any;

// The vampire ignores type safety!
console.log(vampire.name.toUpperCase());

No TypeScript error!

Wait, What?! 🙀

Does that mean the code is safe?

At runtime

TypeError: vampire.name.toUpperCase is not a function

💀 GAME OVER 💀

Count Any didn't turn the number into a string.

He just convinced TypeScript to stop checking it!

That's what makes any dangerous.

It allows operations without requiring proof that they'll work.

But unknown behaves differently.

const visitor: unknown = JSON.parse('{"name":666}');

console.log(visitor.name.toUpperCase());
// ❌ TypeScript stops us!

TypeScript refuses to continue until we check the value.

So how do we defeat Count Any?

With a Type Guard, of course! 😸

import { isString, struct } from "is-kit";

const isFriendlyGuest = struct({
  name: isString,
});

if (isFriendlyGuest(visitor)) {
  console.log(visitor.name.toUpperCase());
} else {
  console.log("🧄 Not tonight, Count Any!");
}

And just like that

THE VAMPIRE HAS BEEN DEFEATED! 🧄🎉

Well, at least this particular cursed value has been rejected.

A Type Guard checks the actual runtime value, while a type assertion only changes what TypeScript believes about it.

One important detail, neither unknown nor any changes the value at runtime.

They are TypeScript types.

The difference is what the compiler allows us to do before verifying the value.

And that's why unknown is usually the safer choice for untrusted data.

😸 Epilogue: We Survived Halloween!

What a night!

We met the Unknown Living Dead, opened a gigantic pumpkin, collected some candy, and defeated Count Any!

So, what did we learn?

Monster TypeScript lesson
🧟 Unknown Living Dead unknown prevents unchecked operations
🎃 Big Pumpkin struct validates object shapes
🍬 Trick or Treat or combines reusable type guards
🧛 Count Any any bypasses normal type checking

Of course, any isn't always evil.

Sometimes it's useful when dealing with legacy code or difficult integrations.

But when working with API responses, parsed JSON, and other untrusted values, keeping them as unknown until validation is usually a much safer approach.

And is-kit makes those checks easy to compose and reuse!

If you want to explore more, check out the official guide 👇

📖 How to Validate unknown in TypeScript Without a Schema Library

And remember

The real monster isn't unknown. It's unchecked any. 🧛

Happy Halloween!!! 🎃👻

If you enjoyed this little TypeScript adventure, check out is-kit!

nyaomaru / is-kit

Build small guards. Compose them. A lightweight, zero-dependency toolkit for building reusable TypeScript type guards that compose, refine, and preserve natural narrowing. Runtime-safe 🛡️, composable 🧩, and ergonomic ✨.

is-kit

Build small guards. Compose them.

is-kit is a lightweight, zero-dependency toolkit for building reusable TypeScript type guards.

is-kit is not just a collection of isX helpers. Its main focus is composing small runtime checks into reusable guards while preserving useful TypeScript narrowing.

It helps you write small isFoo functions, compose them into richer runtime checks, refine properties on values you already know about, and keep TypeScript narrowing natural inside regular control flow. Use it at runtime boundaries when needed, without requiring a schema-first workflow.

Runtime-safe 🛡️, composable 🧩, and ergonomic ✨ without asking you to adopt a heavy schema workflow.

  • Build and reuse typed guards
  • Compose guards with and, or, not, oneOf
  • Use refineKey to narrow a child property while preserving its parent type
  • Validate object shapes and collections when that is useful
  • Parse or assert unknown values without a large schema framework

Thank you for reading! 🤲

articles.title: We took over ChatGPT accounts: the MathLive postMessage chain, and the 20-line audit for your own listeners
articles.description: A shared ChatGPT link, a math keyboard library listening to any sender, an iframe that inherits chatgpt.com, a CSP bypass through YouTube's oembed, and the session token: full account takeover, fixed Oct 26, $5k bounty. The attack chain step by step, and a static audit I ran against the vulnerable library itself: 4 listeners, zero sender checks.
articles.body_html:
Yesterday's disclosure from Parameter is the most elegant web exploit of the month: a complete takeover of ChatGPT accounts where the victim's only action was opening a shared-conversation link. No paste, no login, no click in the final version: about 4.5 seconds from link to JavaScript running as chatgpt.com, reading private conversations and the session token. Reported October 18, escalated from P2 to P1 on October 21, fixed October 26, bounty $5,000. The root is a class of bug almost every web app ships today, which is why this post is the chain dissected step by step, plus a 100-line static audit I wrote and ran against the vulnerable library: it flags exactly the four listeners that made this possible, and your codebase can be scanned the same way tonight.

The chain, in seven moves

The ingredient list: a shared conversation (public feature), MathLive (the math input library ChatGPT loads when a message contains an interactive graph), and the HTML Preview pane that runs on a separate sandboxed origin.

  1. The lure. Attacker shares a conversation containing a real interactive graph (which makes chatgpt.com load MathLive and install its virtual-keyboard message listener) plus an HTML block.
  2. The unguarded door. The sandboxed HTML Preview sends postMessage calls. MathLive's listener never checked who the message came from ("from any web address", per the researchers) and accepted a update-setting message carrying attacker-controlled HTML in the keyboard layouts[].markup field, then a show message.
  3. The sink. The layout renders through keyboardContainer.innerHTML, via a createHTML helper that was a Trusted Types wrapper or identity function, not a sanitizer. I verified the sink in the shipped bundle: s.innerHTML = Qi.createHTML(a) and friends, still present in MathLive 0.100.0.
  4. The origin inheritance. The injected payload is an <iframe srcdoc> without a sandbox attribute. A srcdoc iframe inherits the embedding document's origin: the new frame is chatgpt.com.
  5. The CSP bypass. The Content-Security-Policy blocked inline scripts but allowed YouTube. So the payload loads www.youtube.com/oembed?...&callback=<js>;void, a JSONP-style response whose body begins with attacker-chosen JavaScript. CSP sees a fetch to youtube.com, allowed. The browser executes the callback as script.
  6. The token. Running as chatgpt.com, the code reads the session bootstrap data from the page (#client-bootstrap) and obtains the access token.
  7. The takeover. With the token: GET /backend-api/conversations..., enumerate, read, exfiltrate via an innocent-looking image request. "Any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account."

Every individual piece is a textbook finding. The lesson is the composition: a library's lax listener plus a sandboxed pane plus a permissive CSP plus an unsandboxed srcdoc equals account takeover on the most-visited AI site on earth.

The audit: your listeners, tonight

The bug class has a signature: addEventListener('message', ...) handlers that never reference event.origin or event.source. I wrote a static scanner around that signature (heuristic, minified-bundle-friendly, ~100 lines) and ran it on the two things that matter:

$ python3 postmessage_audit.py mathlive-0.100.0.mjs
[RISK] mathlive-0.100.0.mjs:2841 message listener -> NO SENDER CHECK (.origin/.source absent)
[RISK] mathlive-0.100.0.mjs:2931 message listener -> NO SENDER CHECK (.origin/.source absent)
[RISK] mathlive-0.100.0.mjs:2931 message listener -> NO SENDER CHECK (.origin/.source absent)
[RISK] mathlive-0.100.0.mjs:3084 message listener -> NO SENDER CHECK (.origin/.source absent)

$ python3 postmessage_audit.py mathlive-0.111.1.mjs        # current release
(no message listeners flagged in the main bundle)

$ python3 postmessage_audit.py ~/code/my-app/src/           # your turn

The core of the check (full script embedded below, self-contained):

PATTERNS = [re.compile(r"addEventListener\(\s*['\"`]message['\"`]\s*,"),
            re.compile(r"onmessage\s*=")]
ORIGIN_OK = re.compile(r"(?:event|e|ev|msg|evt)\.(?:origin|source)\b")
DANGEROUS = re.compile(r"innerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|outerHTML|\beval\(|new Function\(")
# for each listener: extract the handler body; flag if ORIGIN_OK absent,
# and flag louder if a DOM sink lives inside the same handler

Honest limits: it is a heuristic on source text (proxy handlers, wrapped frameworks or dynamically-registered listeners can slip through), a clean scan is not a proof, and the runtime gold standard is opening DevTools and watching which listeners react to a synthetic postMessage from a foreign origin. But the pattern it flags is precisely the one that cost OpenAI a P1 this month, and it catches the version that had it while passing the one that does not.

The full script (drop it in a repo or run it in CI over your frontend bundles):

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# postmessage_audit.py <file-or-dir> [...] : flag message listeners without sender checks
import re, sys
from pathlib import Path
RX = [re.compile(r"addEventListener\(\s*['\"`]message['\"`]\s*,"), re.compile(r"onmessage\s*=")]
ORIGIN = re.compile(r"(?:event|e|ev|msg|message|evt)\.(?:origin|source)\b")
SINK = re.compile(r"innerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|outerHTML|\beval\(|new Function\(")
def scan(path):
    try: text = path.read_text(errors="replace")
    except Exception: return
    for rx in RX:
        for m in rx.finditer(text):
            win = text[m.end():m.end()+2000]; depth=0; body=""
            for i,ch in enumerate(win):
                if ch=="{": depth+=1
                elif ch=="}":
                    depth-=1
                    if depth==0: body=win[:i+1]; break
            else: body=win[:1500]
            line = text[:m.start()].count("\n")+1
            v=[]
            if not ORIGIN.search(body): v.append("NO SENDER CHECK")
            if SINK.search(body): v.append("DOM sink in handler")
            if v: print(f"[RISK] {path.name}:{line} -> {'; '.join(v)}")
for a in sys.argv[1:]:
    p=Path(a)
    for f in (sorted(p.rglob("*")) if p.is_dir() else [p]):
        if f.suffix in {".js",".mjs",".ts",".jsx",".tsx",".html",".vue",".svelte"}: scan(f)

The four defenses, in order of leverage

  1. Check the sender, always. First line of every message handler: if (event.origin !== EXPECTED) return;. One line, kills the entire class. That line was missing in a library embedded in one of the world's top websites.
  2. A Trusted Types wrapper that sanitizes, or nothing. createHTML that passes bytes through is a compliance badge on an open door. If you adopt Trusted Types, the policy must actually constrain (DOMPurify or equivalent), not just wrap.
  3. Sandbox your srcdocs. An <iframe srcdoc> without sandbox inherits your origin. sandbox="allow-scripts" (no allow-same-origin) makes the injected document powerless against yours. The preview pane was sandboxed; the attacker's frame was not.
  4. CSP is a budget, audit the allowed list. Any endpoint echoing a callback parameter is a script-execution primitive (JSONP is not dead, it lives in oembed endpoints). youtube.com in a CSP is not "just videos": read it as "YouTube decides what JavaScript runs on my page".

What this means for AI platforms specifically

The trust model of an AI chat app is unusual: user-generated content becomes application UI (shared conversations render graphs, previews, embeds inside the first-party origin). Every library the platform loads to render that content inherits the platform's authority, and the attacker gets to choose which content triggers which library. OpenAI's fix (rejecting cross-frame MathLive messages plus CSP changes) is correct and shipped in eight days. The $5,000 bounty for a full account takeover on the flagship product is, let us note in passing, a curious pricing signal.

TL;DR: a shared ChatGPT link + MathLive's message listener that trusted any sender + innerHTML sink + unsandboxed srcdoc + YouTube JSONP CSP bypass = the session token and every private conversation, patched October 26. The bug class is addEventListener('message') without an origin check; the 100-line audit above flags it in your bundles (and correctly flagged the vulnerable MathLive while passing the fixed one). One line of event.origin validation per listener is the whole vaccine.

Sources: Parameter: We took over ChatGPT accounts · MathLive · audit verified against mathlive 0.100.0 (4 listeners, no sender checks, innerHTML sinks present) and 0.111.1 (pattern absent from main bundle)

articles.title: Debugging in the Agentic Era
articles.description: Coding agents write frontend code fast, but they can't see it run. This is the flow I use to fix...
articles.body_html:
Coding agents write frontend code fast, but they can't see it run. This is the flow I use to fix that, with a signup form that fails on submit as the example.

The Old Way

  1. The agent changes the form.
  2. You open the page, click submit, and nothing happens.
  3. You open DevTools, find a 422 in the Network tab, and copy the response.
  4. You paste it into the chat. The agent guesses a fix.
  5. You reload. Now the console shows a TypeError. You copy and paste again.

You're the agent's eyes, and most of your time goes to copying, not thinking.

The New Way

  1. You ask: "Submit the signup form on localhost:3000 and tell me why it fails."
  2. The agent clicks submit, reads the 422 response and the console, and matches them to the code.
  3. It explains the cause and proposes a fix.
  4. You check that explanation against what you see in the browser, then approve or push back. 
flowchart TB
  accTitle: The old way and the new way
  accDescr: In the old way, the agent writes code, the browser shows an error, and you copy that error back to the agent. In the new way, the agent reads the browser through MCP and reports its findings to you, and you validate them before it continues.
  subgraph Old
    direction TB
    a1[Agent] -- writes code --> b1[Browser]
    b1 -- error --> y1[You]
    y1 -- paste --> a1
  end
  subgraph New
    direction TB
    a2[Agent] -- writes code --> b2[Browser]
    b2 -- MCP --> a2
    a2 -- findings --> y2[You]
    y2 -- validate --> a2
  end
  Old ~~~ New

The copy-paste is gone. You're still there, in a different role.

This is human in the loop (HITL): the agent gathers evidence, and you validate it. Don't trust it 100%. It can misread a trace, or silence an error instead of fixing it.

The HITL notes in this post mark where to look yourself.

Cover Every Scenario

Browser access lets the agent put a page through every scenario your customers hit, not only the one where everything works:

Scenario What the customer should get
Success The flow works end to end
Slow A loading state, no double submits
Error A clear message, their input kept, a retry
Performance Fast loading, no layout shifts
Accessibility Works with a keyboard and a screen reader

The rest of this post shows how to set it up, then walks through each one.

The Tools

Two MCP servers give an agent a browser. MCP is an open standard, so neither is tied to Claude Code. Both work in Cursor, VS Code with Copilot, Codex, and Gemini CLI.

Chrome DevTools MCP

Chrome DevTools MCP is Google's MCP server for Chrome. It lets the agent open pages, click, and read what you see in DevTools:

  • Console: errors, warnings, and logs
  • Network: requests, status codes, and payloads
  • Performance: traces with Core Web Vitals like LCP and CLS
  • Accessibility: Lighthouse audits and the accessibility tree
  • Emulation: slow networks, offline mode, CPU throttling, dark mode, reduced motion, and forced colors

Playwright MCP

Playwright MCP is Microsoft's MCP server for browser automation. It drives Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, can make a single request fail, and helps the agent write end-to-end tests you can rerun.

Installing Them

Most agents read the same config:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome-devtools": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
    },
    "playwright": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest", "--caps=network"]
    }
  }
}

The --caps=network flag turns on Playwright MCP's request mocking. In Cursor, add the config under Settings > MCP. In VS Code, both READMEs have one-click install buttons.

In Claude Code, two commands add both:

claude mcp add chrome-devtools --scope user npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest
claude mcp add playwright -- npx @playwright/mcp@latest --caps=network

Run /mcp to confirm they're connected. Then ask the agent to open your local app and list the console messages.

By default, Chrome DevTools MCP starts its own Chrome. To use the one you already have open, add --autoConnect. It needs Chrome 144 or later, with remote debugging allowed at chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging.

Which One When

Use both, for different jobs. Chrome DevTools MCP looks inside one page: debugging, comparing, and measuring. Playwright MCP fails requests on purpose and writes tests you can rerun in any browser.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a browser MCP server
  accDescr: To debug, compare pages, or measure performance in Chrome, use Chrome DevTools MCP. To write end-to-end tests, mock failed requests, or check Firefox and Safari, use Playwright MCP.
  need{What do you need?}
  need -- "debug, compare,<br>measure" --> devtools[Chrome DevTools MCP]
  need -- "e2e tests, mocks,<br>other browsers" --> playwright[Playwright MCP]

The Debug Loop

Start with the success path: the flow working end to end. With browser access, getting there follows the same loop every time.

The agent changes the code, reloads the page, and reads the signals. You review what it found and steer it when it chases the wrong cause.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: The debug loop
  accDescr: The agent edits the code, reloads the page, and reads the console, network, and performance trace. You review what it found. If the issue isn't fixed, you steer the agent and it edits again. When it's fixed, you ship.
  edit[Agent edits code] --> reload[Reload page] --> read[Agent reads signals]
  read --> review[You review findings]
  review --> fixed{Fixed?}
  fixed -- no, you steer --> edit
  fixed -- yes --> ship[Ship]

HITL: Keep the browser window visible while the agent works. When it says the bug is fixed, reproduce it yourself before you believe it.

The two signals you'll read most are console errors and network requests.

Console Errors

My prompt: "Open /signup, submit the form, and list the console errors. Explain the cause before changing anything."

The agent reads the error and its stack trace, opens the file it points to, and tells you what it thinks went wrong. You read that explanation before any code changes.

HITL: An error that disappears isn't always fixed. Check the diff: the agent may have wrapped it in a try/catch or removed the code that logged it.

Network Requests

My prompt: "Submit the form and show me the request and response for /api/signup. Compare the payload with what the backend expects."

The agent lists the requests, opens the failing one, and compares its body with the code that builds it. A misnamed field or a missing header shows up right there.

HITL: Check the request against the API spec, not the agent's reading of it. Changing the frontend to accept a broken response hides a backend bug.

Testing Slow and Failing Requests

Customers rarely see a crash. They see a failure handled badly: a spinner that never stops, a blank page, a form that loses what they typed. The agent can slow things down or break them on purpose and show you what customers see.

Each server does this differently:

  • Playwright MCP fails one request: browser_route makes an endpoint return a 500, a 404, or a malformed body.
  • Chrome DevTools MCP degrades the whole page: emulate sets Slow 3G, offline mode, or CPU throttling. It can't mock a single request.

My prompt, combining both: "Make POST /api/signup return a 500, submit the form, and screenshot what the user sees. Then try it on Slow 3G."

Slow

On Slow 3G or with the CPU throttled, check what the customer gets:

  • A loading state that shows up right away and ends, with an error if it takes too long
  • A submit button they can't press twice
  • Content that doesn't jump around when it arrives

Error

With a request failing, check what the customer gets:

  • A message in plain words that says what to do next, not a stack trace or raw JSON
  • Their input still in the form
  • A retry that works
  • Focus moved to the error, and the error announced to screen readers

Once a state looks right, lock it in with Playwright's page.route() so it stays that way:

test('signup keeps the input and offers a retry when the API fails', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.route('**/api/signup', (route) => route.fulfill({ status: 500 }));
  await page.goto('/signup');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('ada@example.com');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign up' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Try again');
  await expect(page.getByLabel('Email')).toHaveValue('ada@example.com');
});

HITL: The agent can confirm an error message appears. Only you can judge whether it helps. Read each error state as a customer would: is it clear, kind, and does it say what to do next?

Improving Core Web Vitals

Slow requests are one side of speed. The other is how fast the page loads and settles, and that's where browser access helps most.

Without it, the agent guesses from the code. With it, the agent records a trace, sees which element is the LCP and what shifts the layout, and measures again after each change.

My prompt: "Record a performance trace of the home page with the CPU throttled 4x. Tell me the LCP element and what shifts the layout, then suggest one change at a time."

That turns "this might be faster" into numbers. The agent proposes a change, reruns the trace, and keeps it only if LCP or CLS improves.

HITL: Read the trace yourself before accepting a change. One run is noise, so ask for several. And the trade-offs are yours: preloading an image or inlining CSS can win a metric and cost something else.

Checking Accessibility

An accessible page works for every customer: people on a keyboard, on a screen reader, or who need more contrast or less motion. The agent can check part of this in the browser.

Chrome DevTools MCP runs a Lighthouse audit and reads the accessibility tree, the names and roles a screen reader announces. It also turns on the settings some customers rely on: forced colors, higher contrast, and reduced motion.

My prompt: "Run a Lighthouse accessibility audit on /signup, then tab through the form and tell me where the focus goes."

Lock the fixes in with axe in your Playwright tests:

import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('signup has no detectable accessibility violations', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze();
  expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
});

HITL: Automated checks catch only some accessibility issues. A clean audit doesn't mean the page works with a screen reader. Tab through it yourself, and try VoiceOver or NVDA on the flows that matter.

Migrating Legacy Code Without Regressions

A migration has to keep every scenario working. The worst migration bug is a new page that looks almost like the old one, so capture how the legacy page behaves before you change anything.

Start with a Contract

Write down what must stay the same. This is the contract, and every test after it checks against it.

## Contract: /checkout

- Same visible text and layout at 390px and 1280px
- Same API requests, in the same order, with the same payloads
- No new console errors or warnings
- LCP and CLS no worse than the legacy page
- Every action reachable with the keyboard

The idea is the same as in MigFlow: agents need a contract, not a tutorial.

HITL: You write or approve the contract. The agent can draft it from the legacy page, but it can't know which behavior your users depend on.

Cover the Legacy Page with Tests

Many legacy projects have no end-to-end tests. With Playwright MCP, the agent walks through the legacy page in a real browser and writes a Playwright test for each line of the contract.

Run them against the legacy page first. They must pass there, so they describe what the page does today, quirks included.

Playwright's toHaveScreenshot() saves screenshots of the legacy page as the baseline. Visual changes then show up as a pixel diff, not a judgment call:

test('checkout looks the same as the legacy page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout.png', { fullPage: true });
});

Create the baseline from the legacy page with npx playwright test --update-snapshots. After that, every run compares against it.

HITL: Read every test. A test that passes no matter what protects nothing. Some quirks it captures are bugs you'll want to fix, not keep.

Migrate and Rerun the Same Tests

Now migrate, and run the same tests against the new page. A failing test is a regression. When one fails, the agent uses Chrome DevTools MCP to compare both pages and find out why.

The tests stay in CI after the migration, so the next change is covered too.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: Migrating without regressions
  accDescr: Write the contract, then cover the legacy page with Playwright tests. Migrate the code and run the same tests. If they fail, debug with Chrome DevTools MCP and migrate again. When they pass, you review and ship.
  contract[Write the contract] --> cover[Test the legacy page]
  cover --> migrate[Migrate the code]
  migrate --> pass{Same tests pass?}
  pass -- no --> debug[Debug with DevTools MCP]
  debug --> migrate
  pass -- yes --> review[You review and ship]

HITL: When a test fails, you decide whether the page or the test is wrong. Don't let the agent update a screenshot baseline or loosen an assertion to go green without your OK.

Limits

  • The agent can be confidently wrong. It will explain a wrong cause as clearly as a right one.
  • It's slower than reading the code when the bug is obvious.
  • Traces and logs fill the context window, so ask for the specific signal you need.
  • The agent can read cookies and local storage. Add --isolated for a temporary profile, and be careful with --autoConnect, which uses the Chrome you're signed in to.
  • Performance traces may send page URLs to Google's CrUX API. Add --no-performance-crux when you debug internal URLs.

Try It

Start with one prompt in any agent: "Open localhost:3000, list the console errors, and explain the cause before fixing anything."

Then try the other scenarios on one page: "Load the checkout page on Slow 3G, then with the payment request failing, and screenshot what the customer sees in each case."

Migrating a page? Write the contract, then ask: "Write Playwright tests for this contract and run them against the legacy page." Run the same tests after the migration.

A Tool in the Engineer's Hands

Success, slow, error, performance, accessibility: the agent can now put a page through every scenario and bring you the evidence. That's a powerful tool in the engineer's hands.

It doesn't decide what the evidence means. Every HITL note above comes down to the same habit: keep your eyes on the browser, and treat the agent's conclusions as claims to check, not facts.

As I wrote in AI Writes Code. You Own Quality., speed without judgment means shipping bugs faster. Browser access doesn't change who owns the fix. It gives you better evidence to own it with.

The agent gets eyes on the browser. You keep the judgment.

articles.title: I made $0 from my side project for 8 months. Then one furious email at 2am changed everything.
articles.description: For eight months, the most-visited tab in my browser was a Stripe dashboard that said $0.00.  I'd...
articles.body_html:
For eight months, the most-visited tab in my browser was a Stripe dashboard that said $0.00.

I'd open it first thing in the morning, the way other people check the weather. Refresh. $0.00. Refresh again, because maybe it hadn't loaded. $0.00. Then I'd close it, open my editor, and go do the thing I was sure would finally move that number: ship another feature.

I shipped a lot of features. Dark mode. A second onboarding flow because I didn't like the first. CSV export nobody asked for. A settings page with toggles for things that didn't need toggling. I posted on launch-day forums. I rewrote the landing page headline four times. I A/B tested a button color like the button color was the problem.

Eight months. Roughly thirty features. Exactly zero dollars.

And then, in a single week, it stopped being zero — not because of a feature, a growth hack, or a headline. Because of one furious email at 2am. I want to tell you exactly what that email changed, because it rewired how I think about building anything, and it's the opposite of every "just ship more" post you've ever scrolled past.

The thing I was actually doing for eight months

Here's the uncomfortable reframe, and it took me far too long to see it.

For eight months, I was producing output. A feature is output. A settings toggle is output. A fourth headline is output. Every one of those thirty things was a real, deployed, working piece of software that existed because I typed it into being.

And output — the typing, the scaffolding, the "make a thing that exists" — is the part that got free. I was writing most of that code with an AI by then, shipping faster than I ever had in my life. I could produce a polished feature in an afternoon. I was a one-person feature factory running at full tilt.

$0.00 is exactly what a feature factory running at full tilt is worth, if that's all it is.

Because the number on the dashboard was never waiting on another feature. I kept treating $0 as a production problem — not enough shipped, not polished enough, not enough toggles — when it was never a production problem at all. The hard part of a product was never the code, and it definitely isn't the code anymore. The hard part is a single stranger caring enough to depend on the thing, come back to it, and be genuinely hurt when it breaks. I had compressed the easy 20% — the building — to almost nothing, and spent eight months doing more and more of it, while the impossible 80% sat there untouched.

I wasn't building a business. I was building a very productive graveyard, one tombstone a week.

What the 2am email actually was

I had a free trial. A handful of people had started one over those months — I'd watch them poke around for ten minutes and vanish. Output going out, nobody depending on it. Fine. Zero.

Then one trial user did something none of the others had: they used it. For real. Put their actual work in it, came back the next day, and the day after. One stranger, finally leaning their weight on the thing I'd made.

And the thing I'd made had a bug I'd shipped months earlier and never noticed, because noticing it required someone to actually depend on it. I had a write path that acknowledged the request before it had actually persisted the row. In the demo, in my tests, on my machine — flawless. It had been "flawless" for eight months precisely because no real weight had ever been on it.

Then a retry hit at the wrong moment. The ack went out — saved! — and the save didn't land. This user got locked out of their own account, with no record that they'd ever done the thing they'd just spent an evening doing. Ack-before-persist. Their work, gone, and the app cheerfully telling them it was fine.

The email came in at 2am. It was furious, and it was right to be furious.

And I'll tell you the truth about how that felt, because it's the whole point of this post: it was the first time in eight months that anything I'd built had mattered enough to make someone angry. Thirty features, and not one of them had ever cost a real person a bad night. This one bug had. For the first time, there was a human on the other side of the glass who could be hurt by my mistake — and was.

What I did next was the only thing that ever moved the dashboard

I didn't ship a feature. I was awake anyway.

I found the bug — the ack-before-persist — fixed the write path so the acknowledgement could not possibly go out before the row was durably written, backfilled the data I could recover, and replied to the email. Not a templated apology. The actual explanation: here's what broke, here's why, here's exactly what I changed so it can't happen to you again, here's what I could recover and what I couldn't.

That user wrote back. Stayed. Converted when the trial ended. And — this is the part that still gets me — told two other people, both of whom became the first paying customers I ever got who weren't me testing my own Stripe integration.

The dashboard stopped saying $0.00.

Not because of a feature. Because for the first time I had done the one thing I'd avoided for eight months without even realizing I was avoiding it: I let a real stranger get close enough to hurt me, and then I stood in the consequence instead of shipping away from it.

Output vs. judgment — the distinction that was hiding in the whole thing

Here's the line I wish someone had put in front of me on month one:

Shipping a feature produces output. Shipping to a user who can hurt you produces judgment. Output is free now. Judgment is the entire game.

Thirty features risked nothing. Not one of them could churn, refund, rage-email me, or lock themselves out at 2am. They were safe, which is exactly why they were worthless — I was manufacturing output in a room where nothing could ever go wrong, and calling the $0 a mystery.

The bug was the first thing I ever built that could go wrong on a real person. And the fix — the staying, the reply, the standing-in-it — was the first time I made a judgment that cost me something. That single scar taught me more about my own product than the previous eight months of building combined. It also, not coincidentally, was the first thing that made anyone pay.

That's the math nobody prints on the "ship every week" poster: eight months of output that couldn't hurt me earned $0. One night of judgment that did earned the first real dollar.

To be clear — this is not "stop shipping"

I need to be fair here, because the lazy version of this post is "features are bad, slow down," and that's wrong.

I am not telling you to stop building. I ship constantly. I let an AI write most of my code and I would never go back — it's the reason I could produce thirty features in eight months, and I'm glad I can. Building is fast and cheap and good, and you should do it.

What I'm saying is narrower and, I think, more useful: features were never the bottleneck, so producing more of them was never going to move a number that was stuck for a completely different reason. The scarce thing — the only thing that was ever going to turn $0 into not-$0 — was a real person depending on the thing and me surviving the consequence when it broke. AI made the output free and did absolutely nothing about that. It can't. Nobody can generate another human's dependence on you for free.

So ship. Ship fast, with the machine, joyfully. But know which part is the free part, and do not mistake eight months of the free part for eight months of progress.

Why this is the exact reason I build the way I do now

Here's the part that goes one level up, because it's the same lesson wearing a different hat.

I build an agent platform now, and the whole industry's reflex this year is to celebrate the author — the thing that generates. Look how fast it ships! Thirty features in eight months, a whole app in an afternoon! But an author running at full throttle, with nothing checking it, produces exactly what I produced: infinite output, zero judgment, and a dashboard that says $0. My eight months were a one-person preview of what unchecked generation gets you.

So I never let the thing that writes the code be the thing that blesses it. There's an author that produces the diff — fast, tireless, free. There's a separate skeptic whose only job is to ask the question I never asked for eight months: what does this do if the write gets retried? And there's a human on the merge button who owns the 2am, who can see the blast radius the model can't. Author, skeptic, human. That separation is the entire shape of xenition — and it's the same thing the $0 dashboard taught me the hard way: generating the thing is free and always will be; deciding whether it survives contact with a real person is the whole job, and the only part anyone ever pays for.

My side project didn't make $0 because it was missing a feature. It made $0 because for eight months it was all author and no skeptic, all output and no judgment, and nothing in it could hurt me. The day one thing finally could — and I stood in it — the number changed.

Build one thing that can hurt you. Then stay for the 2am. That's where the dollar is.

articles.title: Halls of Horror: Build a Haunted House with Gemma, Then Dare Your Friends to Walk It

articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

I've always treasured Halloween. It's my favorite holiday. My dad and I share the same love for Halloween - I definitely inherited the love from him. I mean, there is a reason why I have Freddy and Jason tattoos!

I remember going to Netherworld for the first time back in college, 16 years ago. It was my first haunted house! I've gone almost every year since. I went to a few different haunted houses but nothing beats the best. I am so fond of it. The art. I view haunted houses as the ultimate art form. Netherworld just knocks it out of the park each year. They are the true masterminds of the art of Halloween.

I'm truly sad to miss this year because I’m recovering from ankle surgery but I will be back next year!

I wanted to build an app as an homage to my love for haunted houses and storytelling.

So I built Halls of Horror: a haunted house builder where Gemma, running right in your browser, is the creative director.

  • Pick your nightmare: an abandoned asylum, a carnival that never left town, a hotel with a sealed 13th floor, a toy shop after dark… or dream up your own
  • Choose how scary: Cozy creepy, Creepy or Terrifying
  • Gemma builds the haunt: the legend guests hear in line, then room after room of what they see, what they hear, the scare and the scare actor's line
  • A secret 13th room: behind the last room waits a locked door, with a twist ending you only see at the very end
  • Walk it: a dark, flickering hallway, room by room, with a flashlight that follows your mouse and creepy sound made live in your browser. No audio files at all.
  • Every character screams their own way: the ghost wails, the doll giggles, the clown laughs, the witch cackles, the shadow growls, the captain moans and the bellhop rings his bell
  • Sound captions: every scream, the thunder and the 13th door show up as text, so the scares work on mute too
  • Survive it: make it out and you get a card with the rooms you walked, the scares you survived, and whether you found the secret room, plus a button to share the haunt
  • Share it: send a link and your friends can walk your haunt, no download needed
  • Print the actor script: every room as a script for real scare actors. Home haunters, this one's for you.

How I read the theme: "Ghost in the Machine" is the ghost writer living in your browser. Gemma dreams up the haunt, and the walk-through puts you inside it.

Demo

Live app: https://halls-of-horror.onrender.com (Chrome or Edge on a laptop works best. Click "walk through a sample haunt" to try the walk-through without downloading Gemma.)

Code

tmott13 / halls-of-horror

🕯️ Gemma builds you a walk-through haunted house, right in your browser. Pick a theme, get a legend, rooms full of scares, and a secret 13th room. Painted scenes, a flashlight mode, character screams, and sound captions. No server, no sign-up. Built with Angular + WebLLM.

Halls of Horror

Build a walk-through haunted house with Gemma. Then dare your friends to walk it.

Pick a nightmare (an abandoned asylum, a carnival that never left town, a hotel with a sealed 13th floor…), choose how scary, and Gemma, running right in your browser, writes your haunt: the legend guests hear in line, then room after room of what they see, what they hear, the scare and the scare actor's line. Behind the last room waits a locked 13th door with a twist ending.

Then take the walk-through: a dark, flickering hallway, room by room, with creepy sound made live in your browser (no audio files). Share a link and your friends can walk it too, no download needed.

Live: halls-of-horror.onrender.com · Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

How it works

  1. Design: pick a theme (or dream up your…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Open model: Gemma 2 2B (gemma-2-2b-it-q4f16_1-MLC) on laptops, with Gemma 3 1B as the lighter option for phones.
  • Runs in the browser: WebLLM runs Gemma on your GPU with WebGPU. It downloads once and is cached, so building works offline.
  • Sound: all synthesized with the Web Audio API: a low drone, wind, heartbeats, creaks, a detuned music box, a carnival waltz, and a different scream for each character.
  • Frontend: Angular 22 with signals, plus the Creepster and Special Elite fonts.
  • Hosting: a free static site on Render, with no backend at all.

Like my last four projects, the big idea is Gemma writes the words, and the app owns everything else:

  1. One room at a time. A 2B model loses the thread if you ask for a whole haunted house at once. So Gemma builds one room at a time, and each one sees the legend and the rooms before it. They stay on theme and never repeat.
  2. A simple format the app can always read. Gemma answers in ROOM / SEE / HEAR / SCARE / LINE. The app reads it even when Gemma adds bold or numbers, and fills in anything missing, so a room never breaks.
  3. The app picks the sound. If Gemma writes about a calliope, the room gets the carnival organ. Dripping water gets drips, whispers get whispers. Gemma never touches the audio.
  4. The twist is its own step. The secret 13th room gets its own prompt: it sees every room and has to flip the legend.
  5. Spooky, not gory. Every prompt asks for PG-13 haunted-house fun: no gore, no real people, no real tragedies. And before you enter, a warning screen lets you turn off sound or flashing light. Flashing starts off for anyone who prefers reduced motion.

I was surprised how well Gemma created the script for the haunted houses. A true mix of storytelling and spook.

I built this with Claude as my pair programmer. I picked the idea, made the product calls, and tested every haunt myself.

Accessibility

Accessibility is very important to me, which is why I included some methods inside Halls of Horror.

  • A content warning before you enter, with switches for sound, flashing light and the flashlight
  • Sound captions for every scream, the thunder and the door, read out by screen readers too
  • Reduced motion: the shaking, lunging and flickering turn off, and the scares just fade in and out
  • Keyboard friendly: Space, Enter or → to keep walking, Esc to leave
  • Labeled buttons that say whether they're on or off
  • Your choices are remembered
  • A tap finishes the typing so you never wait

Spoiler alert: I will be creating a series soon called Vibe Check. A series on how AI misses the mark on accessibility and how humans are still needed "in the loop". I will also be making some updates to include more accessibility features and attributes to the projects I created for Hacktoberfest this month.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • It runs anywhere, even offline. Once Gemma is downloaded, you could plan a haunt in a basement with no signal, which feels right.
  • It's private. Your haunts are saved in your browser. Even the share link is the haunt, packed into the part of the link after #, which browsers never send to a server.
  • It's free. No API bill and no subscription, so home haunters and families can play with it all October.
  • It won't disappear. No service to shut down. The model, the code and your haunts are all yours.
  • I control the whole pipeline. I decide what Gemma sees, how it's broken into steps, and the safety rules around it.

The Spirit of It

In the spirit of Halloween, I hope this brings you a spark of joy or even a scare! I loved being able to share my love for Halloween with you! I enjoyed being able to combine my passions of tech, art, and storytelling together with my favorite holiday.

Prize Categories

  • Gemma: Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 1B run fully in the browser with WebLLM, writing the legend, every room and the secret 13th room.
  • Render: deployed as a free Render static site from a render.yaml blueprint.

Thanks to DEV, the Hacktoberfest team, and the MLC/WebLLM and Gemma teams. Happy Halloween!

articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine    ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Séance Shell is a haunted terminal. A small ghost lives in your Bash or Zsh session, watches for the moments that matter, and murmurs a single eerie sentence about what just happened.

It reacts to two kinds of events:

  • Destructive-looking commands like git reset --hard, git clean -fd, or rm
  • Failed builds and tests like pytest, npm run build, or cargo build

Once the command has finished, the ghost speaks:

$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
ghost: the past has accepted your changes, and forgotten your future.

That's the whole product. The ghost is a companion for reflection, not an assistant for execution. It never suggests commands, never runs anything, and never offers advice.

How I read the theme: the prompt suggested "a haunted terminal that possesses your shell and whispers back eerie commentary." I wanted that, but with restraint. Most AI tools are loud and eager to help. A good ghost lingers at the edge of the room, says one unsettling thing, and goes quiet. Séance Shell is a ghost that knows its place.

Code

0shuvo0 / seance-shell

Séance Shell 👻

A quiet, local-AI terminal companion that offers one short reflection after selected commands. The ghost is atmospheric, not an assistant: it gives no advice, runs no generated text, and never retries a command.

$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
ghost: the past has accepted your changes, and forgotten your future

Reflections are generated independently by Ollama on your machine with gemma3:latest. Model output is validated before display. If the local model is unavailable, the reflection is skipped.

What it does

  • Notices selected destructive-looking commands and failed build/test commands.
  • Reflects only after the shell has already completed a command; it never re-runs it.
  • Sends Ollama a category, outcome, and—only for an explicit seance reflect --context request—short sanitized context. Shell hooks do not send the command text to the model.
  • Requires one sentence, at most 15 words and 180 characters; malformed output is discarded.
  • Uses dim terminal text when…
View on GitHub

To run it locally you need Ollama and the gemma3:latest model. The shell hook works without the model, so the ghost only goes silent if Ollama isn't running.

How I Built It

The open-source pieces are what make this work:

  • Ollama runs inference locally.
  • Gemma 3 (gemma3:latest), Google's open-weight model, is the default.
  • A Bash/Zsh hook detects events after the shell has finished a command.

No cloud API, no hosted inference, no account. Three design decisions shaped the build.

1. The model never sees your command

The shell doesn't send the raw command string to the model. It sends a structured description:

  • category: destructive or failed-build
  • status: succeeded or failed
  • context: optional, and sanitized first

The model gets enough to set a mood but nothing it could be tricked by or leak. It is not a coding agent and can't be steered by arbitrary shell content.

2. The output is validated aggressively

The model is asked for one sentence, at most 15 words and 180 characters. If the response is malformed, multi-line, or too long, it's discarded and the ghost stays silent. The text on screen is a constrained artifact, not whatever the model felt like saying.

3. A ghost, not an agent

Séance Shell never retries commands, never executes anything, and never reinterprets what you did. It's a passive observer. That modesty is what makes it usable in a place where you're making decisions at speed.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A terminal is about as personal as software gets. It holds your file paths, repo names, half-finished experiments, and the commands you'd rather not explain. An always-on ghost watching that is only acceptable if it lives on your own machine.

Open-weight models made that possible in three ways:

  • It works with the lights off. There is no network call in the loop, so the ghost haunts you on a plane, in a basement, or during an outage.
  • Your context stays on your machine. Even with command text withheld, I wouldn't want a terminal's activity flowing to a server I don't control. With a local model I don't have to take anyone's word for it, and I can read exactly what gets sent.
  • I control the personality. The ghost's voice depends on the prompt, the validation rules, and the model. With open weights I can swap Gemma for another model or tighten the constraints without asking a vendor, and nothing can be deprecated out from under it.

A closed API could have written the sentences. It couldn't have given me a ghost that is private, offline, and mine, and that's the part that makes it feel like a haunting rather than a service.

The Spirit of It

The first time it fired, I ran git reset --hard HEAD~1 on a throwaway branch and the ghost answered: "the past has accepted your changes, and forgotten your future." It was a small moment, but the one-line reminder that I had just erased something did what no warning dialog ever has. It made me pause.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 3 runs locally through Ollama as the model behind every one of the ghost's reflections.

articles.title: Architecting a Fair 24-Hour Launch Engine with React, Firestore, and Google AI Studio: An Engineering Retrospective (Astro Discover)
articles.description: As developers, we've all been there: you spend 3 to 6 months building something useful, you submit it...
articles.body_html:
As developers, we've all been there: you spend 3 to 6 months building something useful, you submit it to traditional launch platforms, and within three hours you're buried under VC-funded tools, sponsored upvotes, and timezone cutoffs.

Instead of just complaining about it, I decided to engineer a technical solution: Astro Discover — a clean product discovery engine and launchpad with a synchronized 24-hour spotlight window.

Here is an honest engineering retrospective of how I architected this using React, Vite, Firebase Firestore, and Google AI Studio, including the hard constraints and edge cases we solved.

1. System Requirements & Core Constraints

Before writing code, I set three non-negotiable architectural requirements:

  1. Deterministic 24-Hour Windows: Products must not launch at arbitrary hours. Every scheduled product must go live at exactly 12:01 AM IST and stay on the front page for 24 continuous hours.
  2. Fail-Safe Queue Processing: If a manual security review is pending when the scheduled launch date hits, the system must not delay the launch. It must automatically display the project with a "Pending Review" badge.
  3. Sub-Second TTFB & Direct Hydration: No flashy loading overlays, no bloated client-side trackers. Immediate first contentful paint.

2. The Tech Stack & Architecture

Frontend: React + TypeScript + Vite

  • Zero-Flicker Routing: Core pages (Home, Today, Explore) are bundled directly for instant initial paint, while secondary management routes (Admin, Dashboard, Bug Reporting) are code-split using dynamic imports.
  • Tailwind CSS Utility Styling: Clean dark/light theme tokens without external component framework bloat.
  • Deterministic Date Utilities: We wrote custom normalization helpers (parseFirestoreDate and isScheduledOrCreatedTodayIST) to ensure browser timezone offsets never cause hydration mismatches or Invalid Date crashes.

Backend: Real-time Reactive Firestore

  • Firestore provides real-time snapshot listeners for upvotes and submissions without having to maintain a dedicated WebSocket fleet.
  • Firestore Security Rules enforce strict role-based access control (RBAC), ensuring makers can only modify their own submissions and upvotes cannot be artificially spoofed.

3. Engineering Challenges We Solved

The Timezone Normalization Problem

When makers schedule from San Francisco (PST) vs London (GMT) vs Tokyo (JST), raw JavaScript new Date() calculations can split a launch across two calendar dates.

We solved this by anchoring our launch engine strictly to Indian Standard Time (IST, UTC+5:30) at the data layer. Dates are stored as canonical YYYY-MM-DD strings alongside epoch timestamps, guaranteeing that every user across the globe sees the exact same daily launch batch.

Eliminating Client-Side "Loading Jitter"

During early prototyping, we had temporary Suspense fallback spinners showing "Loading..." screens. For a developer audience, that feels slow and unpolished.

We reworked the component tree:

  • Empty states and skeleton placeholders are kept minimal and inline.
  • Root HTML is completely clean, allowing the React tree to hydrate directly with zero flashing text or spinners.

4. Key Takeaways for Solo Builders Using AI Studio

Building a production-ready application with Google AI Studio taught me a few crucial lessons:

  1. Design the schema first: AI performs best when you give it clear interfaces (e.g., explicit TypeScript types for Project, LaunchStatus, StartupStage).
  2. Own your edge cases: AI will scaffold standard CRUD operations effortlessly, but timezone math, security rules, and queue fallbacks require human oversight and precise constraints.
  3. Focus on developer utility: Features like 1-click tech stack inspection, GitHub repo links, and license filtering resonated far more with users than fancy animations.

Try Astro Discover

The platform is open, active, and live right now:

Is This Course for You?

This course is for you if:

  • You know JavaScript and want to learn TypeScript
  • Your team uses TypeScript and you want to understand it properly

You do not need any TypeScript experience. If JavaScript is also new to you, start with the free JavaScript course first.

What Is TypeScript?

TypeScript is JavaScript with types. You describe what your data should look like, and TypeScript checks your code before it runs.

Here is a small example from Session 09. An order can have only four statuses, and someone makes a typo:

type OrderStatus = "pending" | "paid" | "shipped" | "cancelled";

interface Order {
  readonly id: number;
  status: OrderStatus;
}

const order: Order = { id: 1001, status: "pending" };
order.status = "shiped";

TypeScript catches the mistake before the code ever runs, and even suggests the fix:

error TS2820: Type '"shiped"' is not assignable to type 'OrderStatus'. Did you mean '"shipped"'?

In plain JavaScript, the wrong status would be saved without any warning, and someone would find the bug much later. TypeScript is built to catch mistakes like this early.

The Final Project

node -v

You need version 24 or newer. If you don't have it, install the LTS version from nodejs.org.

Step 2: Create a practice folder. Make a folder called ts-practice and open it in VS Code (File > Open Folder).

Step 3: Open Session 01. Read it and do the "Try It Yourself" part. Session 02 then installs TypeScript with you, step by step.

Tips to get the most out of it

  1. Go in order. Every session builds on the ones before it.
  2. Type the code yourself. Don't copy and paste. Typing helps you learn.
  3. Check and run. Run npx tsc to check your code and node to run it, then compare with the session.
  4. Do the exercises before you move on to the next session.

At one session a day, most learners finish in 6 to 7 weeks.

Yes. No signup, no paywall, no email list.

No. Everything is written, with animated diagrams for the hard parts, so you can learn at your own pace.

I have never used TypeScript. Can I follow it?
Yes. Session 01 starts from zero. You only need basic JavaScript.

My company uses an older version of TypeScript. Is this still useful?
Yes. The language is the same, and the course points out the places where older versions behave differently.

Please open an issue on GitHub. Every report helps the next learner.

articles.body_html:
Everyone posts haunted house stories today. Mine are less atmospheric. In every one of them, the thing that broke the client's site was me.

Here are five, in no particular order of shame.

1. "It's live, check it out"

I sent the client a message saying the changes were done. The client opened the site and saw the old version.

The cache was holding on to the old site, and I was holding on to the belief that I had deployed. Only one of us was right.

2. Lorem ipsum, live and in production

Placeholder text is supposed to be replaced before anyone sees it. Mine made it onto the live site.

3. It ran fine on my phone

I checked the mobile version on my own phone, saw it working, and moved on. The client opened it on an older phone and it fell apart. Turns out "works on my phone" is just "works on my machine" with a smaller screen.

4. The animation that ate the battery

It looked great on my laptop, smooth and exactly what I wanted.

On a phone it heated the device and drained the battery.

5. The environment variables that weren't there anymore

I overwrote the environment variables on production. Yes, the real ones.

None of these needed a full moon. Just me, convinced it was fine.

What's the scariest thing you've shipped yourself?

articles.body_html:
Every photo you take on a phone carries a small dossier inside the file: the exact GPS coordinates where you stood, the device that took it, the software version, the capture time, and sometimes even the camera's serial number. Most people never see any of it, because image viewers don't show it. But anyone you send the original file to can read it in seconds.

That's why I built Drop Metadata, a free tool that strips hidden metadata from photos and videos without ever uploading them.

What's actually hiding in your files

Here's the kind of thing a single phone photo can reveal:

Field Example
GPS 37.774887, −122.419388
Device iPhone 15 Pro
Software iOS 17.2
Captured 2026-01-15 10:30:00
Serial Camera / lens serial number
C2PA AI provenance manifest

Post that photo of your new desk setup or your kid's first day of school, and you may have shared your home address along with it.

Drop Metadata removes all of it: GPS coordinates, camera make and model, capture software, timestamps, author and copyright fields, camera and lens serial numbers, XMP editing history, and C2PA content credentials.

Why "no upload" was non-negotiable

Most free "metadata remover" sites work by uploading your file to their server, cleaning it there, and sending it back. That means the very file you're trying to protect, GPS location and all, gets handed to a stranger first.

So the core rule for Drop Metadata was simple: the file never leaves your device.

  • The file is read straight from disk into browser memory. No network request is made.
  • Every embedded field is listed by category before anything is removed, so nothing is stripped blindly.
  • The clean file is rebuilt locally and downloaded straight back to you.

No upload, no account, no server, no copy of your file anywhere. A nice side effect: it's instant, because there's no upload or download round trip.

Zero quality loss

A lot of tools "remove" metadata by re-encoding the whole image, which quietly degrades quality every time. Drop Metadata doesn't touch the pixels.

Metadata lives in its own containers, separate from the image or video data: EXIF and XMP segments in JPEGs, metadata chunks in PNGs, and metadata boxes inside MP4/MOV files. Drop Metadata rewrites only those containers and copies pixel data and video samples byte for byte. Nothing is re-encoded, so the output is visually identical.

It works on video too

Video is the part people forget. Phones embed GPS and device tags inside MP4 and MOV containers as well. Drop Metadata cleans them at the container level, so location and device tags are stripped without re-encoding a single frame, and the file size stays effectively identical.

Supported formats: JPG, PNG, MP4, MOV, any size.

📱 Get the Android app

Most of the photos worth worrying about never touch a laptop. They go straight from your camera roll to a marketplace listing, an email attachment or a "send as file" chat. So I built Drop Metadata for Android to clean them right where they live.

  • See before you strip. The app lists every field it finds by category, and plots the photo's GPS location on a map, before anything changes.
  • You choose what goes. Each category has its own switch. Remove the location but keep the date, clear the camera details but keep your copyright, or wipe everything in one tap.
  • Photos and videos. JPEG, PNG, MP4 and MOV. Video is cleaned at the container level, so no frame is re-encoded.
  • Fully offline. No server, no account, no sign-up, and it works with no internet connection at all. The Play Store data-safety label says no data collected and none shared.
  • No quality loss. Pixels and video frames are copied byte for byte, and photo orientation is preserved, so portrait shots stay upright.

A quick reality check on "but social media strips metadata anyway": the big platforms usually do, as a side effect of re-encoding. Email, messaging apps sending files, cloud links, marketplaces and forums usually don't. Cleaning the file before it leaves your phone is the only reliable approach.

  1. Install it and open a photo straight from your camera.
  2. Tell me in the comments which fields it found, and whether anything looked wrong or missing.
  3. Try a video too, and let me know your phone model if anything breaks.

Bug reports are just as welcome as praise.

Try it
