articles.title: All That Glisters Is Softmax: Shiny-Object Interns, Airplane-Magazine Execs, and Why AI Labs Can Only Bake In Half the Scars
articles.description: Why do an eager intern with a Hacker News blog post, a C-level executive stepping off an airplane with an in-flight magazine, and a trillion-parameter LLM all walk straight into the exact same production bog? And why even Google DeepMind can only bake half of our 600 scars into model weights.
articles.body_html:
Why do an eager intern with a Hacker News blog post, a C-level executive stepping off an airplane with an in-flight magazine, and a trillion-parameter LLM all walk straight into the exact same production bog? Because for 3,000 years of human literature—and in every softmax attention matrix—the shiniest path is a trap.

"All that glisters is not gold; / Often have you heard that told." — William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice (Act II, Scene VII)

"While many say THIS leads to THAT, I'm here to say THIS should lead to THE OTHER." — Randal L. Schwartz (The 12-Word Definition of a Synthetic Scar)

1. The Power Loader vs. The Passenger Seat: Why We Use Human Psychology to Debug QK^T / sqrt(d_k) Matrices

Whenever a skeptic looks at an AI coding workflow, their first accusation is predictable: "You outsourced your thinking to a stochastic parrot."

My answer is the exact opposite:

I didn't outsource the thinking—I outsourced the typing. It's my thoughts. Always.

Think of the hydraulic Power Loader exo-suit from Aliens—or a Pacific Rim Jaeger. When you step into a Power Loader, the machine does not decide where the cargo goes. Every micro-movement of the hydraulic arms is a 100x mechanical amplification of the human operator's nervous system, bounded by physical safety interlocks so the hydraulics cannot crush the pilot.

Over 246 production tickets (142 open-source framework tickets across BlocSignal, kaisel, and our research tools + 104 commercial enterprise industrial tickets) and 600 codified Synthetic Scars (577 public at syntheticscars.org + 23 private domain invariants), our repeat regression rate on previously scarred failure modes has remained locked at 0.0% (68.3% autonomous first-pass verification, N_nudge = 1.91 mean human nudges per ticket).

Yet when developers read the formal preprint on syntheticscars.org or browse the previous installments of this series, they often ask a fascinating question:

"Randal, why are you using Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker neuroscience, John Grinder and Richard Bandler's 1975 NLP Meta-Model, Gregory Bateson's cybernetics, Fernando Flores's 1986 speech-act commitments, and Baron-Cohen's Sally-Anne Theory of Mind test to debug a matrix multiplication (softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V) running on a Google TPU?"

Because of The Corpus Mirror Isomorphism:

  1. The Weights Are Fossilized Human Psychology: A foundation model is a compressed statistical hologram of trillions of tokens of unedited human thought, rationalizations, Stack Overflow shortcuts, and cognitive biases. When you multiply Q x K^T, you are running a linear-algebra simulation of human System 1 associative attention (Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow).
  2. Damasio's Patient "Elliot" in Silicon: In Descartes' Error (1994), neuroscientist Antonio Damasio studied patients with ventromedial prefrontal and amygdala lesions who retained 100% intact IQ and logical reasoning, yet destroyed their lives because they lacked somatic markers—the visceral gut recoil ("I have a bad feeling about this") that prunes catastrophic options before conscious calculation begins. An unscarred LLM is Damasio's patient at scale: encyclopedic recall of every algorithm on Earth, paired with zero amygdala.
  3. Why Prose "DON'T" Rules Fail (Hypnotic Priming in Self-Attention): In The Structure of Magic (1975) and Trance-formations (1981), Grinder and Bandler observed that the human nervous system cannot represent a linguistic negation ("Don't think of a pink elephant", "Don't spill the milk") without first activating the internal sensory representation of the forbidden act. In a Transformer, placing "DO NOT use .asData?.value" or pasting a 10-line "// BAD: DON'T DO THIS" snippet into your .cursorrules loads the exact forbidden syntax tokens into the Key-Value (KV) cache, boosting their cosine similarity in the next attention head!
  4. Machine Theory of Mind & The Sally-Anne False-Belief Test in transcript.jsonl: Why does a single-window agent fail to catch its own bugs when you tell it "Now review your own code"? Because in psychology's classic Sally-Anne test (Baron-Cohen, Leslie, & Frith, 1985), once you know the marble was moved to the box, it takes deliberate cognitive effort to simulate an observer who only sees the closed basket. In an LLM's single context window, the Builder's private rationalizations ("I skipped the null check because the caller probably validates it") sit right there in the KV cache (E_Builder). When you fork an isolated Target 40 Clean-Room Critic Subagent (Workspace: 'inherit') that sees only the Git Merkle tree diff (git write-tree) and the 4-Vector Scar Registry (E_Critic orthogonal to E_Builder), you physically enforce the Sally-Anne separation.

2. The Four Isomorphic Hazards: The Intern, The Executive, The Cargo Cultist, and The Softmax Voter

Once you realize that an unscarred LLM is a pure System 1 associative engine with zero skin in the game, you immediately understand why managing AI coding agents feels eerily familiar to every veteran engineering manager.

Four personas we deal with every week in software engineering are mathematically isomorphic:

flowchart TD
    I["1. The Shiny-Object Intern\nReads a weekend Hacker News blog post;\nrewrites core loop on Monday"]
    E["2. The Airplane-Magazine Executive\nReads glossy in-flight success story;\ndemands Friday migration"]
    C["3. The 'Next-Model' Cargo Cultist\nDatamines IDE configs for leaked codenames;\nblames model when 150k-token prompt collapses"]
    L["4. The Unscarred Softmax Sampler\nSamples top-1 web tutorial popularity\nP(token) = Majority Vote of Page-1 Google"]

    Bog["💥 The 3 AM Production Bog\n(Leaked streams, race conditions, unindexed queries, silent data drops)"]
    I --> Bog
    E --> Bog
    C --> Bog
    L --> Bog

    Barrier["🛡️ The Synthetic Scar & Makefile Airlock\n• 4-Vector Scars: THIS → NOT THAT → THE OTHER\n• Target 40 Clean-Room Critic ('Sam at the end of the hall')\n• SHA-256 Witness Receipts & Turn-Key Human Gates"]
    Bog -. "Target 90 Post-Mortem (12s Scar Compilation)" .-> Barrier

Hazard 1: The Intern with a Bright Shiny Object (And Why Checklists Fail without "Sam at the End of the Hall")

Every senior lead has mentored the brilliant, energetic intern who reads a clever Hacker News blog post over the weekend and comes in Monday morning having rewritten the production message bus using a shiny new reflection trick—completely oblivious to the memory leaks and teardown deadlocks waiting at 3 AM.

Now ask yourself: how do you stop a hasty intern from shipping broken code?

  • If you hand the intern a sheet of paper with 15 checkboxes ("Did you check blast radius? Did you write sad-path tests? Did you check stream disposal?") and say, "Check these boxes before you talk to me," what does an impatient intern do? They go ☑ ☑ ☑ ☑ ☑ in three seconds and hand you the paper!
  • Single-agent prose checklists in CLAUDE.md or .cursorrules fail for the exact same reason. Telling the same model that just wrote the code to "self-certify" its own checklist is asking the intern to grade their own homework.
  • How do you manage the intern? You tell them: > "Please go away until Sam at the end of the hall has signed off your changes—and don't come back without Sam's cryptographic receipt."

In our Makefile DAG (WORKFLOW.mk), Sam at the end of the hall is the isolated Target 40 Six-Pillar Adversarial Critic Subagent paired with deterministic compiler and AST gates. The Builder subagent cannot advance to Target 45 (human-review-approval) or Target 50 (commit) without a verified 40_critic_review.md receipt locked to the exact git write-tree Merkle hash (SCAR-GIT-23).

Hazard 2: The C-Level Executive with an Airplane Magazine

A C-level executive steps off a cross-country flight holding a glossy in-flight magazine article titled "How Enterprise X Replaced Their Entire Backend in 3 Days!" and demands the engineering team adopt it by Friday.

Why is the airplane-magazine article so seductive? Because magazine writers—just like tutorial bloggers—edit out all the ugly parts. Nobody writes an in-flight magazine feature about the 14 weeks spent debugging distributed lock starvation, schema migration rollbacks, or zombie WebSocket descriptors.

Hazard 3: The "Next-Model" Cargo Cultist ("Wait for Next Week's Leaked Codename!")

Spend five minutes on AI Twitter or Reddit today and you will meet the 2026 cousin of the airplane-magazine executive: the developer who spends all day datamining IDE configuration files for unreleased model codenames ("Okay, now we have Argon, but what we really need is Carbon / Next-Flash / Claude-Next / GPT-Next!").

Whenever their 150,000-token single-window "vibe coding" session collapses into an apology loop, their diagnosis is always the same: "The current model got nerfed! Wait until next Tuesday's model drop!" They are convinced that when they drive their 2026 sports car off a cliff because the road has no guardrails, the solution is trading it in for a 2027 sports car with 200 more horsepower.

A faster cosine-similarity engine trained on the exact same 10 trillion happy-path tutorials will drive off the exact same sad-path cliff—just at twice the tokens per second.

Sometimes people ask me: "Randal, why do you care how strangers on the internet prompt their AI agents? Let them vibe-code if they want!"

My answer is simple civic self-defense:

I care because I will always be forced to use mobile apps, banking portals, medical systems, and websites that I did not create. Single-prompt vibe coding without sad-path engineering is flooding the public software commons with fragile, insecure software that breaks the moment reality deviates from the sunny day.

Hazard 4: The Unscarred LLM ("Popularity Is the Weights of LLMs — We Don't Code by Majority Vote")

For decades, when competing as a consultant against cheaper "new talent," my pitch was simple—I would point to my arms and say:

"You're not paying me for what I can do; you're paying me for what I know not to do—and I've got the scars to prove that."

Watch what happens when a junior developer searches Google for "how do I do X in Flutter / Python / TypeScript":

  • They look at the first page of 10 Google results and assume they are ranked from best to worst.
  • When a 40-year senior architect looks at those exact same 10 results on Page 1, they immediately cross 4 of the 10 off on sight (-∞) as "very bad, unsustainable, will deadlock under load, or a nightmare to maintain"—because they have lived through what happens six months after you copy-paste them.

Now think about how a Large Language Model is trained. Cross-entropy pre-training optimizes next-token probability P(x_t | x_<t) to match corpus frequency.

"Popularity" is literally the weights of an LLM. And we don't code by majority vote.

An unscarred LLM's highest-probability completion (Vector 2: The Trap / [5, 6, 7, 8]) is the most frequently copy-pasted tutorial answer on Page 1 of Google! Neither the tutorial blogger, the airplane-magazine writer, the eager intern, nor the stateless token sampler is on the 3 AM PagerDuty rotation (Nassim Nicholas Taleb's Skin in the Game). Without a SCAR_REGISTRY.md to veto those 4 toxic Page-1 candidates (-∞), a "smarter" LLM is just a faster typist for the majority-vote mistake.

3. 3,000 Years of Literature Warned Us About Softmax (Vector 2: The Trap)

Why did we call Vector 2 of every Synthetic Scar The Trap (The Seductive 5-6-7-8)? Because long before Geoffrey Hinton or Ashish Vaswani wrote down the softmax equation (P(y_i | x) = exp(z_i / tau) / sum_j exp(z_j / tau)), three thousand years of human folklore, mythology, and literature were already warning us about greedy local reward maximization:

Literary / Mythological Archetype The Seductive Happy-Path Lure (Vector 2: The Trap) The Hidden Production Catastrophe (Vector 1: The Wound) The Structural Countermeasure (Vectors 3 & 4: Circuit Breaker + Reflex)
Shakespeare's Three Caskets (The Merchant of Venice, Act II) The Gold Casket: "Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire" (Literally Softmax Majority Vote!) Inside the gold casket is a carrion skull and the scroll: "All that glisters is not gold." The Lead Casket: Dull, unglamorous, inscribed "Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath" (Skin in the Game / TDD + Critic verification).
European Folklore & Tolkien (Will-o'-the-Wisp / Ignis Fatuus / The Dead Marshes) Glowing ghost lights hovering just a few steps off the dark, muddy trail ("Follow the highest local logit!") Stepping toward the light plunges the traveler into a bottomless anaerobic bog. Gollum's rule: "Don't follow the lights!" Keep your eyes locked on the physical stones of the Makefile path.
John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678, By-Path Meadow) The highway is rough and stony (Red-Green-Refactor); right across the stile lies By-Path Meadow, smooth and green, running parallel to the road on Day 1. By nightfall the path curves away from the highway, floods behind you, and traps you in Doubting Castle ("Vibe Coding" at Day 14). Refuse the stile (!Counter-Offer); pay the upfront friction of the stony highway (Target 15 Archaeology → Target 20 Plan → Target 30 Red Test).
Homer's Odyssey (Book XII, The Sirens) The Sirens promise effortless omniscience ("We know all things that shall hereafter be upon the fruitful earth"). Sailors who steer by conversational willpower crash onto the bone-strewn rocks. Beeswax in the crew's ears (15ms AST Sensors + isolated worker contexts) and lashing Odysseus to the mast (Makefile DAG + human turn-key gates).

Look closely at Odysseus and the Sirens. Odysseus did not survive the Sirens by writing "CRITICAL: DO NOT LISTEN TO THE SIRENS" on a sticky note and trusting his willpower while sailing past the island. He knew that once the song entered his context window, his weights would want to steer into the rocks. So he used physical architecture: beeswax for the rowers (ephemeral subagents that never see the bloated chat history) and ropes around the mast (hard Makefile prerequisites that cannot be untied from inside the model).

4. The CISC-to-RISC Agentic Revolution & Why We Already Invented AGI

Over the past two months, as I watched our workflow evolve from a 21-step prompt checklist into a Make-Fork pipeline backed by 600 scars, a realization hit me:

Effectively, high-level languages pushed algorithms down to the macro level. What we're doing is pushing programming down to the macro level. High-level languages fixed the impedance mismatch between the programmer and the algorithm—and moving from monolithic mega-prompts to a Make-Fork pipeline is how we go from CISC to RISC once we realize complex silicon is the expensive part. All I want the LLM to do is compute cosine-similarity. I can handle the sequencing and multipath using the baked-in ancient tech. The question wasn't "how much smarter before AGI" at all. It was "how long before we learn to phrase the questions such that cosine similarity computes it all." — Randal L. Schwartz

Let's unpack why this changes how we view both agent engineering and AGI:

1. The Late-1970s CISC Mistake vs. The 1980s RISC Breakthrough

In the late 1970s, computer architects built CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) chips like DEC's VAX, stuffing massive multi-cycle polynomial evaluators (POLY), procedure call frames (CALLS), and string formatters directly into complex microcode on the silicon die. Then John Cocke (IBM 801), David Patterson (Berkeley RISC), and John Hennessy (Stanford MIPS) proved a revolutionary principle: complex microcode slows down the clock for everything, and the compiler can sequence simple instructions better than silicon.

Look at how 99% of developers run AI coding agents today:

  • They stuff 12 skills, a 2,000-line .cursorrules file, an MCP tool catalog, and 150,000 tokens of history into a single monolithic CISC context window, hoping the neural network will simultaneously simulate a project manager, a state machine, a code generator, a linter, and an adversarial code reviewer in one continuous stream.
  • Forcing an O(N^2) attention matrix on a $40,000 TPU to simulate a for loop and a Makefile is the 2026 equivalent of VAX microcode!

In our RISC Agentic Pipeline (SCAR-PROC-95):

  • The Harness Compiler (WORKFLOW.mk + POSIX state files) handles 100% of the deterministic sequencing, state persistence, SHA-256 Merkle tree locking, and risk-tier routing at zero token cost.
  • The TPU / LLM is used strictly for what it is best at: a single-cycle, fixed-width (15k–25k token) Cosine-Similarity ALU (Free Flow Between the Riverbanks). Production was down, the dashboard was bleeding red, and every suspect had an alibi. The killer had my git credentials.
3:04 A.M.

The phone glows at 3:04 in the morning, and there is a grammar to that light. Not the white of a text from someone who loves you. Not the green of a package arriving. The amber of the paging app — the color of weather emergencies and furnace warnings; the color machines use when they want to inform you, courteously, that something you built is misbehaving in public.

I sat up in the dark and opened the laptop, which lit my face the way open freezers do in films about regret.

The dashboard was a Jackson Pollock painted entirely in red. Our authentication service — the front door of the product, the one service contractually obligated to be boring — was failing at a rate I had previously considered theoretical. Users weren't just failing to log in. They were being logged out. Mid-session, mid-sentence, all across the map, in every timezone our little empire covers.

Every engineer has a private horror story, and we tell them the way fishermen describe weather: exaggerated, semi-mythological, absolutely load-bearing. I want to tell you mine as what it actually was — a horror story — because it has every required element. A remote cabin (my apartment). A storm (rain, theatrical, unpaid). An isolated protagonist (me, insufferable). And a monster no search party could ever find, because I was about to spend four hours learning that the monster had my face and my commit history.

What it doesn't have is a villain. That's the part the genre never prepares you for.

The Fine Art of Needing Someone to Blame

Every incident has a casting call, and mine convened immediately.

Suspect one: the deploy. It is always the deploy; this is the closest thing software has to folk wisdom, and folk wisdom survives because it is usually right. I checked. Nothing had shipped in four days. The most recent release had the alibi of sediment.

Suspect two: the network. "It's not DNS," I told the empty room. "There is no way it's DNS." I checked the DNS anyway, the way you check behind the shower curtain in a horror film — not because you expect to find anything, but because the genre demands one token act of courage. The DNS was fine. Somehow its innocence felt like a betrayal.

Suspect three arrived on schedule, and I am not proud of this: the new engineer. She joined three weeks ago. She had shipped nothing, touched nothing, and was, at that moment, asleep like a person with a clear conscience — statistically the most suspicious condition there is. By 3:40 I had mentally drafted a post-mortem with her name in it. Gently worded. Professionally devastating.

Here is what I was actually doing, though I lacked the vocabulary for it at the time: running a comfort ritual. Humans are blame-seeking missiles. Hand us an unexplained catastrophe and we will generate a villain with the reflexive urgency of an immune response. Villains make chaos narratable. A system that failed for seventeen interacting reasons is a nightmare you can't repeat at parties; a system that failed because Dana pushed on Friday is a story, and stories feel like control.

The safety literature worked this out decades ago, in an industry that counts its dead. James Reason's Swiss cheese model — the one from aviation, the one that says disasters happen when the holes in several layers of defense happen to line up — exists precisely because "one careless person" is almost never the truth of a serious failure. Charles Perrow went further in Normal Accidents and argued that in systems complex enough, breakdowns are not anomalies at all. They're residents. They pay rent.

I knew all of this. I had once cited it at an all-hands, in a confident voice, with a slide. At 3:40 A.M., knowledge and comfort are different organs, and only one of them was working.

The Bug With a Bedtime

Salvation, when it came, came from the most suspicious direction available: arithmetic.

Coffee number three had arrived not as a beverage but as a coping mechanism with a handle. I stopped staring at the aggregate error graph — staring at aggregates at 4 A.M. is just doom with a scrollbar — and sliced the errors by hour instead.

And the error rate had a bedtime.

3:00 A.M. Sharp. A spike, a twenty-minute decay, silence. I scrolled back one day: 3:00 A.M., spike, decay, silence. Two days: the same. Seven nights, the same. A metronome wearing a ski mask. Whatever this was, it wasn't random and it wasn't ambient. It was scheduled. Something in my system looked at its watch every night, said now, and did a murder.

Naturally, it refused to happen in staging. I pointed every instrument I owned at the staging environment and it sat there, serene, error-free, smug in the way only a system without real traffic can be. For one feverish hour this felt like a genuine heisenbug — a bug that flees observation, a witness who heard a noise and declines to repeat it. Purists will object that an environment difference is not a true heisenbug, and the purists are right, but at 4:20 A.M. every bug that hides from daylight qualifies as uncanny.

I explained all of this, in detail, to the rubber duck on my desk. His name is Vladimir. He has heard things. He said nothing, which is his gift.

The clue that cracked it was almost embarrassing: the staging servers believed, sincerely and wholeheartedly, that they lived in UTC. The production servers lived in local time. Everything else was identical. Which meant the variable I had been treating as scenery — the clock — was the weapon.

Time zones are the Cthulhu of computing: ancient, tentacled, worshipped entirely by accident. Nobody believes in them until one reaches up out of the deep and takes a production system with it.

A Séance Called git blame

Follow the mechanics forward and the picture assembles itself with the awful neatness of a locked-room mystery finally solved.

The mass logouts came first. The errors were just the thundering herd of evicted users stampeding back toward the door. The logouts were evictions — something was deleting live sessions. And there was only one thing in the entire system with delete rights: a cleanup job, a cron, that pruned "expired" sessions every night while the city slept.

In its WHERE clause, the definition of expired was computed with one clock, while the sessions themselves had been stamped with another. For one window every night, the two clocks disagreed about whether it was still today — and during that window, the job scanned every live session in the database, judged them all ancient beyond recovery, and deleted them. All of them. Then it tidied up, logged its success, and went back to sleep until tomorrow.

And the schedule? The cron ran at 3:00 A.M., because 3:00 A.M. is when traffic is lowest. I know this with terrible intimacy, because I scheduled it there myself, a lifetime ago, in a pull request I described — I checked — as "safe."

One clock stamps. Another clock judges. Once a night, they disagree. The rest is arithmetic wearing a hockey mask.

I ran git blame on the comparison, which is less like forensics and more like a séance: you summon the dead, you ask who did this, and the answer always arrives in monospace. The blame lit up line by line, and then it landed on a commit from 241 days ago, with a message I have now read so many times I've stopped flinching:

quick fix: make cleanup behave for now, will revisit after launch

Author: me. Reviewer: me. And one line above it, written in my exact voice, a comment: // temporary, do not let this ship as-is.

I shipped it as-is.

I want to be precise about the feeling, because "the call is coming from inside the house" is a horror trope for a reason, and the reason is that the house is you. I read that code the way you reread a text you sent at a party: with dawning, pixel-by-pixel horror, at a stranger who had my name, my typing cadence, and my signature joke in the comments. I don't remember writing it. I remember launch week — I remember being exhausted and certain, which is the same memory wearing different clothes. Somewhere between then and now, that line stopped being mine and became the system's. Then the system handed it back to me at 3:04 A.M., with interest.

The Call Was Coming From Inside the Commit

Here is the thing I understood at around five in the morning, sitting in the wreckage of my own certainty — the thing I'd stay up all night again to keep:

A bug is not an intrusion. A bug is a disagreement — the residue left where the system in your head and the system in production quietly parted ways. Alfred Korzybski said the map is not the territory; code is a map we hand to a machine, and the machine is a perfectly literal client. It never rounds up toward our intentions. It executes the gap between what we meant and what we said — at nine digits a second, forever, until somebody notices.

And the noticing is science. Genuinely, structurally science. Every suspect I ran down that night was a hypothesis — the deploy, the network, the innocent new hire — and the logs were nature's answer: no, no, and no. Karl Popper would have recognized the procedure instantly. I wasn't debugging; I was falsifying. I was doing rigorous, disciplined science all night. I just hadn't expected the final theory to be me.

That's the twist the genre keeps missing. We tell debugging stories as detective stories — find the culprit, restore order, roll credits. But there is no culprit, because the culprit is a condition: complexity plus time plus a confident human moving quickly. Edsger Dijkstra — who never once let a good sentence go unsaid — put the quiet part loudly: "Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence." Absence of bugs cannot be demonstrated. Only deferred. Every codebase is a haunted house where all the ghosts are future versions of the people currently alive.

Douglas Hofstadter wrote whole beautiful books about systems that contain their own self-reference — loops that point at themselves and turn strange. We ship those weekly. We just call it Tuesday.

So I gazed into the stack trace, and the stack trace gazed back into me, and it used my font.

Absolution Is Not a Deploy

The fix was one line. I want that on the record, because the disproportion is both the punchline and the lesson: a week of 3 A.M. pages, four hours of dread, one small theological crisis — resolved by teaching two clocks to agree. One word, effectively. Eight months of latent catastrophe, priced at less than a tweet.

Then I did the three things that actually mattered, none of which were the line of code.

I made staging's clocks match production's, because "works in staging" should at minimum mean "works on the same planet." I added an alert on mass logouts specifically, because error rates are the scream and logouts are the whisper, and monitors that only hear screams will always fail you at exactly the volume that matters. And I wrote the post-mortem, and I put my own name in the root cause field.

That last one is the bravest sentence in engineering: I did this. Not as penance. There were no robes, no ritual shaming, no wheel-of-misfortune slide at the all-hands. Blameless doesn't mean consequence-free — it means the consequence is knowledge. The document said, plainly: a well-meaning engineer, under launch pressure, shipped a temporary change with no ticket, no reminder, and no monitoring that could have caught it for 241 days. Remove any one of those conditions and the incident doesn't happen. Which means the fix was never "be more careful." The fix is "build a system where careful is not a heroic act."

Reason's Swiss cheese, again: I wasn't the hole. I was the unlucky alignment of the holes, wearing a lanyard.

At 6:40 the sun came up, indifferent, like a build that passes on the second try. I bought the new engineer a coffee and told her she'd been acquitted of a crime she never knew she was charged with. She laughed. Then she made me show her the diff, and she asked the question every senior engineer should be asked monthly:

"Who else has a TODO like this?"

We found four. Each had my fingerprints, or hers, or someone's — because that is what fingerprints are. Evidence that a human was here. And humans are how the future pages you.

Epilogue for the Next One

The next horror story has no villain either. Statistically speaking, it's you.

Not because you're careless — because you're fast, and confident, and navigating a map so much larger than any territory one person can hold. Seniority in this field isn't the accumulation of tricks. It's the slow, expensive process of updating your priors against your own evidence. Every scar is data. Every 3 A.M. is a peer review conducted by a merciless machine.

So, some benedictions — cheap, and hard-earned:

Write TODOs with dates, not vibes. Temporary, in production, means geological. Schedule your crons at hours you have personally witnessed while awake. And mistrust any diff you'd describe as "safe" in a pull request titled "small cleanup" — the monster is always introduced as a minor character.

The bugs of the future are being written right now, by people who are certain. The only defense our species has found is humility with instrumentation: assume the map is wrong, watch the territory, and when something finally pages you at 3 A.M., skip the séance. Open the blame. Say hello to the author.

Your turn: tell me about your 3 A.M. monster in the comments. I promise I won't ask who wrote it.

The answer is always the same.

articles.title: AI Is Writing More Code Than Ever. But Are We Becoming Better Developers?
articles.description: AI can write code in seconds.  It can build a React component, create an API, fix bugs, generate...
articles.body_html:
AI can write code in seconds.

It can build a React component, create an API, fix bugs, generate database queries, write tests, and even work across an entire codebase without requiring a developer to touch every file.

A few years ago, these tasks could take hours or even days.

Today, an AI coding agent can complete a surprising amount of that work with a simple instruction.

But there is a question we should be asking:

If AI is making it easier to write software, are we actually becoming better software developers?

Or are we simply becoming better at asking machines to write code for us?

This is one of the biggest questions facing the software development industry in 2026.

1. AI Has Fundamentally Changed How We Write Code

Let's be honest. Software development is changing faster than many of us expected.

Tools such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, and other AI-powered coding assistants have changed the traditional development workflow.

Previously, developers generally followed a familiar process:

  • Understand the requirements.
  • Research the solution.
  • Write the code.
  • Debug errors.
  • Write tests.
  • Review and improve the implementation.
  • Deploy the application.

Now, a developer can describe a feature in natural language and ask an AI agent to handle several of these steps.

For example, instead of manually creating an authentication system, a developer might ask:

"Build a complete authentication system with email verification, password reset, secure sessions, and database integration. Follow the existing project architecture."

An AI coding agent can inspect the repository, create files, modify existing code, and propose an implementation.

The developer's role is increasingly shifting from writing every line to directing, reviewing, and validating the work.

This is not a small improvement to the development process.

It is a fundamental change in how software gets built.

2. The Numbers Show How Quickly AI Coding Is Growing

This transformation is not just based on personal observations.

GitHub's 2026 Octoverse report, published on October 28, provides some interesting numbers.

According to the report:

  • Developers pushed 17.9 billion times to GitHub over the reporting year.
  • GitHub recorded 34.3 billion commits across public and private repositories.
  • More than 1.3 billion pull requests were merged.
  • In September 2026, more than 40% of pull requests started with an AI agent, compared with 17% in March.

Think about that last number.

In just six months, the share of pull requests started by AI agents more than doubled.

AI is no longer simply suggesting the next line of code. It is increasingly participating in real software development workflows.

Developers are delegating tasks, reviewing generated implementations, and managing multiple AI-assisted workflows.

The industry is moving from AI-assisted coding toward AI-assisted software engineering.

Source: GitHub Octoverse 2026 coverage

3. The Biggest Risk: Developers May Stop Understanding Their Own Code

Here is where things become interesting.

AI can generate code quickly, but generating code and understanding code are two very different things.

Imagine a junior developer building an application with an AI coding agent.

The agent creates:

  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Database models and migrations.
  • API endpoints.
  • Frontend components.
  • Payment integration.
  • Error handling.
  • Automated tests.

The application works during initial testing.

The developer feels productive.

But what happens when something breaks in production?

What happens when two database operations create a race condition?

What happens when an API exposes sensitive information?

What happens when a subscription is charged twice?

What happens when a seemingly harmless change breaks another part of the application?

If the developer cannot understand the generated implementation, they may struggle to identify the actual problem.

This is the difference between producing software and engineering software.

AI can help you build something. It cannot automatically make you responsible for understanding what you have built.

That responsibility still belongs to the developer.

4. Writing Less Code Does Not Mean Understanding Less

I don't believe developers need to stop using AI to become better engineers.

In fact, avoiding AI completely could become a disadvantage.

The important thing is how we use it.

Consider two different approaches.

Developer A:

  • Gives AI a large task.
  • Accepts all generated changes.
  • Runs the application once.
  • Assumes everything is correct.
  • Moves to the next feature.

Developer B:

  • Understands the requirements before using AI.
  • Provides the correct architectural context.
  • Reviews the generated implementation.
  • Checks database changes and API behavior.
  • Tests edge cases.
  • Examines security implications.
  • Understands the final code before merging it.

Both developers use AI.

Both may produce features quickly.

But their engineering skills are developing in very different directions.

Developer A is becoming dependent on generated output.

Developer B is using AI to increase productivity while continuing to develop technical judgment.

That distinction will matter more as AI agents become capable of handling larger tasks.

5. Debugging Is Still One of the Most Important Developer Skills

There is something interesting about software development.

Writing the first version of a feature is often easier than maintaining it.

A feature might work perfectly with normal input but fail under unexpected conditions.

For example:

  • A user submits the same payment request twice.
  • Two users update the same database record simultaneously.
  • A network request times out after the server has already processed it.
  • An authentication token expires during an important operation.
  • A database migration works locally but fails in production.
  • A background job processes the same task multiple times.

These are not necessarily problems that can be solved by generating more code.

They require understanding how systems behave.

Developers need to understand:

  • Data flow.
  • Database transactions.
  • Concurrency.
  • API contracts.
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Logging and monitoring.
  • Error handling.
  • System architecture.

AI can help investigate these problems, but developers must still evaluate whether the proposed solution is correct.

In an AI-driven development environment, debugging may become even more valuable because more generated code means more implementations that need careful verification.

6. The Junior Developer Problem Is Real

One concern I hear frequently is:

"If AI can write code, how will junior developers gain experience?"

Traditionally, junior developers learned through smaller tasks.

They fixed bugs, implemented simple components, wrote basic queries, and gradually learned how larger systems worked.

These tasks helped them understand the foundations of software engineering.

But if AI handles every small task, developers may miss opportunities to build those foundations.

A junior developer who asks AI to explain a database query and then studies the execution is learning.

A junior developer who copies the generated query without understanding it is missing an important opportunity.

The solution is not to ban AI from junior developers.

Instead, companies and senior engineers should encourage them to:

  1. Attempt small problems independently before asking AI.
  2. Ask AI to explain why a solution works.
  3. Review generated code line by line.
  4. Learn debugging instead of immediately requesting a complete rewrite.
  5. Understand the architecture behind the features they build.
  6. Practice solving problems without AI occasionally.

The goal should be to create developers who can work with AI, not developers who cannot work without it.

7. What Skills Will Matter Most for Developers in 2027?

The definition of a strong developer is changing.

Knowing programming syntax will remain useful, but it will not be enough.

I believe these skills will become increasingly important.

1. System Design

Understanding how frontend applications, backend services, databases, APIs, and infrastructure work together.

2. Code Review

Being able to identify incorrect assumptions, unnecessary complexity, security problems, and performance issues in AI-generated code.

3. Debugging

Understanding why something fails instead of repeatedly asking AI to generate another solution.

4. Security

Knowing how authentication, authorization, data validation, encryption, and secure API design work.

5. AI Agent Management

Learning how to break large tasks into smaller steps, provide context, manage agent workflows, and verify results.

6. Product Thinking

Understanding what users actually need, why a feature matters, and whether the implementation solves the real problem.

7. Independent Problem-Solving

Being able to reason about a technical problem without depending entirely on an AI-generated answer.

These skills complement AI rather than compete with it.

8. AI Should Make Developers More Capable, Not More Dependent

I use a simple principle when thinking about AI-assisted development:

Never merge code that you cannot explain.

You do not necessarily need to type every line yourself.

You do not need to memorize every framework function.

You do not need to manually create every component or database migration.

But you should understand the important decisions behind the implementation.

If an AI agent changes your database schema, understand the migration.

If it modifies authentication, understand the security implications.

If it creates an API, understand the request, response, validation, and error-handling behavior.

If it builds a feature, understand how that feature interacts with the rest of your application.

Use AI to remove repetitive work, accelerate research, explore alternative implementations, and improve your workflow.

But do not outsource your engineering judgment.

That is the skill that makes you a developer rather than simply an operator of coding tools.

9. My Prediction: The Best Developers Will Become AI-Orchestrated Engineers

I don't think AI will simply eliminate the need for software developers.

I think it will change what makes someone a valuable developer.

In the past, productivity was often associated with how efficiently someone could write, debug, and deliver code.

In the coming years, productivity will increasingly involve how effectively someone can:

  • Understand a complex problem.
  • Design a reliable solution.
  • Delegate suitable tasks to AI agents.
  • Coordinate multiple development workflows.
  • Review and validate generated implementations.
  • Maintain systems over time.
  • Take responsibility for the final product.

One developer with strong engineering fundamentals and effective AI workflows may be able to accomplish work that previously required a much larger team.

But that does not mean engineering knowledge becomes less important.

It may become more important.

When AI can generate hundreds of lines of code in minutes, knowing whether those lines should exist in the first place becomes a valuable skill.

Final Thoughts

AI is making software development more accessible, faster, and increasingly powerful.

That is a good thing.

More people can experiment with ideas, build applications, automate workflows, and solve problems that previously required extensive technical knowledge.

But we should not confuse faster code generation with better engineering.

A developer who understands the system, questions assumptions, reviews implementations, and takes responsibility for the final result will always have an advantage over someone who blindly accepts generated code.

We are entering an era where writing code may become less of a bottleneck.

Understanding, designing, reviewing, and maintaining software will matter even more.

The question is no longer just how much code you can write. It is how well you understand the software you create.

And perhaps that is what will separate great developers from everyone else in the AI era.

What Do You Think?

I would love to hear other developers' experiences.

  1. Are AI coding agents making you a better developer, or are you becoming more dependent on them?
  2. Should junior developers learn programming fundamentals before using AI coding tools?
  3. Will system design, debugging, and code review become more valuable than writing code?

Share your thoughts in the comments. I am especially interested in hearing from developers who are already using AI agents in real production projects.

articles.title: TEAM Portability: Six Months of Rebuilding How I Work with AI
articles.description: I thought AI retraining would mostly mean learning to produce software faster: pick the right model,...
articles.body_html:
I thought AI retraining would mostly mean learning to produce software faster: pick the right model, wire up agents, and let throughput carry the rest.

Six months later, I've rebuilt how I work with AI across Codenames AI (an online word game), automated writing workflows, dependency management, and the tools supporting them. Along the way, I've published weekly field reports on DEV.to documenting what broke and what I learned.

The bigger change was not typing speed. It was how I decide what software should do, how I verify it, where I place trust before I merge or ship, and how I carry those habits from one codebase to the next. Looking back across those field reports, I started seeing the same questions recur. Those questions eventually became four recurring disciplines: Taste, Evals & Verification, Authority, and Measurement. Portability became the fifth: making those practices work consistently across projects, tools, and agents. Together, I think of them as TEAM Portability. I did not design that map upfront; it emerged from what kept breaking once the tooling started working.

Taste

Reloading a Codenames AI tab restored the board while leftover targeting highlights lit up cards I had never clicked on the new board. The persisted game state was truthful; the drafting UI was lying about what I had targeted. I found that while exercising mode switches locally, but green CI had nothing to say about the mismatch.

The problem went beyond clearing stale highlights. I had to decide which parts of a player's work should survive a reload and which were temporary drafting intent. I ran into a similar gap when a resume generator passed every pipeline check but still produced something I wouldn't submit.

Both experiences showed me that correct implementation isn't enough when the product requirements are incomplete. Tests can verify the behavior we've specified, but I still need to decide whether that behavior makes sense for the person using the product.

Evals & Verification

While building my writing workflow, I discovered that one strong published example communicated my expectations better than an expanding collection of writing rules. It was easier to show the AI what good writing looked like than to describe every decision behind it.

Evaluating that writing presented a different challenge. My AI reviewer gave a draft 23/25 while missing important editorial problems. I changed the reviewer to analyze drafts before scoring them, so the assessment followed an editorial read rather than driving it.

Even that wasn't enough. As I continued refining the reviewer, I found that separating different kinds of reasoning worked better than expanding the rubric. Challenging an initial assessment, identifying redundant prose, and checking whether a section served the reader each needed deliberate attention.

Together, these experiences changed how I approach evaluation. Clear expectations matter, but so does the process used to assess whether they're met. I still need to decide what quality looks like for a particular task and whether the checks can recognize it.

Authority

While building Savepoints, I expected the agent host to provide reliable lifecycle signals for deciding when completed work needed review. The host didn't. Events were available, but I couldn't safely infer everything I needed about which work had finished or which repository it affected.

Other projects exposed different kinds of missing boundaries. A multi-step agent plan listed every step except where to stop, and an agent merged a PR I expected to review. Separately, Git reported success while hooks never ran in a worktree that lacked the required executable shims.

These weren't identical failures, but they challenged the same assumption: that a boundary existed because I'd described or configured it. I now make execution authority explicit, establish which host signals I can rely on, and check that safeguards actually operate in the environment doing the work.

Measurement

On Codenames AI, the Active players tile looked convincing until I asked which sessions belonged in the number. The dashboard was counting events correctly, but it couldn't distinguish production players from activity on preview deployments. I was reading the number as evidence of real players without knowing which environments contributed to it.

Other experiments exposed different ways that apparently useful signals could mislead me. A production model swap surfaced contract and validation gaps, making it difficult to separate model performance from weaknesses in the surrounding application. And when a Sankey chart of my job applications disagreed with the underlying records, I had to distinguish problems in the data from problems in how it was transformed and displayed.

The common lesson wasn't that the numbers were wrong. It was that interpreting them required understanding what they represented, how they were produced, and which assumptions sat between the underlying events and the result I was looking at.

Portability

I first tried to solve portability by copying one repo's agent setup into the next. That worked until assumptions tied to each product and shared workflows started drifting apart. I eventually separated reusable policy and procedures from the tools and mechanics that belonged to each repository.

That solved how to share the methodology, but not how to keep individual repositories aligned with it. Plans still drifted until structure became checkable in CI. The validator couldn't judge whether a plan was good, but it could verify that the required structure was present.

Working with a remote cloud agent exposed another boundary. Briefing it felt like onboarding a new hire because it didn't automatically inherit my local reasoning or authenticated tools. That separation required a more deliberate handoff, but also made independent execution possible.

Portability, I've learned, isn't copying the same configuration everywhere. It's carrying the same engineering expectations into different environments while accounting for what each environment needs to establish independently.

Six months in, with more to build

Over the past six months, I've experimented with AI across different projects and kept running into the same questions: what outcome matters, what evidence proves it, where the agent must stop, what the numbers actually count, and whether those practices survive in the next codebase.

There's still plenty I want to build and learn, but I'm heading overseas for a few weeks. Six months felt like a good point to reflect on what I've learned so far. When I return, I'll have TEAM Portability as a framework to approach new problems, test what I've learned, and refine my practices as I go.

Takeaway: Getting better at AI-assisted engineering isn't just about learning new tools or producing software faster. It's about developing the judgment to define good outcomes, verify results, set boundaries, understand measurements, and carry those practices into new environments.

articles.description: This is a summary of my original writeup, for the complete technical aspects, including the hardware...
articles.body_html:
This is a summary of my original writeup, for the complete technical aspects, including the hardware investigation, UART access, bootloader exploration, firmware limitations, and the decisions that led to the final network architecture, read the original article: https://medium.com/@hiruthicsha/i-tried-to-hack-my-isp-router-it-turned-into-a-very-expensive-lesson-86cbdbba1fe7

It started with a fairly ordinary problem: random ping spikes while gaming.

Whenever someone at home started streaming 4K videos, my gaming experience would take a hit. The ISP-provided router offered practically no control over bandwidth allocation, device prioritization, or traffic shaping.

I could change the Wi-Fi name. That was about it.

Naturally, instead of buying proper networking equipment, I decided to repurpose an old ISP router that had been lying around after the ISP discontinued the service and told us we could dispose of it.

The plan was simple: install custom firmware, unlock the device, and turn it into something I could actually control.

What followed was a rabbit hole involving hardware hacking, embedded Linux, bootloaders, serial consoles, and a few questionable engineering decisions.

Getting Inside the Router

The first challenge was understanding what I was dealing with.

The router wasn't running some ordinary, easily replaceable Linux distribution. It used a heavily customized firmware built around Realtek's proprietary SDK.

There was no straightforward OpenWRT installation or convenient firmware image waiting to be flashed. So I opened the device, identified the UART pins, soldered headers onto the board, and connected a USB-to-TTL adapter to access its serial console.

After a fair amount of trial and error, I managed to get readable boot logs, interact with U-Boot, investigate the partition layout, and eventually gain deeper access to the device.

There were plenty of small victories along the way, including bypassing restrictions that prevented even basic operations such as resetting the router.

But getting inside the device was only the beginning.

The Difference Between Access and Control

One of the more interesting discoveries was how much control the ISP retained over the device.

The firmware supported remote provisioning, allowing the ISP to push configurations that could overwrite locally configured settings.

This made sense from an ISP's operational perspective, but it also highlighted how little control the end user actually had over hardware sitting inside their home.

Even with elevated privileges, I wasn't necessarily in control of the entire system.

The deeper I investigated, the clearer the limitations became.

The device relied on proprietary drivers, closed-source components, vendor-specific configurations, and a very particular boot and partition structure.

There was no compatible custom firmware available that I could simply install.

Getting OpenWRT or another custom distribution running would require considerably more work, potentially including reverse-engineering missing components and rebuilding significant parts of the firmware.

I had managed to get access to the machine, but that didn't mean I could make it do what I wanted.

The Actual Problem Wasn't the Router

After spending several days investigating the hardware, I stepped back and reconsidered the original problem.

The issue wasn't really the router. It was bufferbloat.

When multiple devices started consuming bandwidth, network queues filled up, increasing latency and causing those frustrating ping spikes.

The router was doing what many consumer routers do: maximizing throughput without providing meaningful traffic fairness or queue management.

What I actually needed was:

  • Traffic shaping to manage network congestion.
  • Per-device bandwidth controls.
  • Traffic prioritization for latency-sensitive applications.
  • Firewall rules and DNS-level filtering.

Trying to force all these capabilities into a locked-down ISP device was the wrong approach.

Moving Network Control Somewhere Else

Instead of replacing the ISP router's firmware, I decided to introduce a dedicated network management layer.

The plan was to let the ISP ONT continue doing what it was designed for: providing internet connectivity.

The actual network management would move to a separate machine running OPNsense.

Fortunately, I already had a mini PC running as a home server, so I could reuse existing hardware rather than purchase an entirely new router.

This approach would give me a proper firewall, traffic shaping, bandwidth management, and more flexibility without having to fight the proprietary internals of the ISP device.

There was one more complication: my mini PC had only a single network interface.

I explored VLANs and router-on-a-stick configurations, but couldn't get the setup working reliably. Eventually, I decided to buy a network switch to make the physical topology more practical.

Interestingly, the old ISP router wasn't entirely useless after all. It could still serve as a wireless access point, while the second router I had initially planned to repurpose as a switch remained an open question.

What I Took Away From This

The project didn't end with custom firmware running on the old router. In that sense, the original objective failed.

But it taught me a few things that I probably wouldn't have learned by simply buying a better router.

  1. Access doesn't equal control.

Getting root access, understanding the bootloader, and manipulating flash partitions doesn't mean you can freely modify a system built around proprietary components.

  1. Understand the actual problem before choosing the solution.

I spent days trying to modify a router when the underlying problem was network congestion and bufferbloat. The right solution was at a different layer of the network.

  1. Sometimes the correct engineering solution is less exciting.

A dedicated firewall and a network switch aren't nearly as interesting as reverse-engineering an ISP router. But they solve the problem without requiring me to rebuild half the vendor's firmware.

  1. Hardware is cheaper than engineering time. Sometimes.

I spent hours trying to avoid buying a switch and ended up ordering one anyway. Whether that was a waste of time or a learning experience is still up for debate.

What's Next?

The next step is to put the new network topology together, get OPNsense running properly, and see whether the proposed setup actually fixes the latency problems.

There are still plenty of things to experiment with: traffic shaping, VLANs, DNS filtering, wireless access points, and network monitoring.

The original plan didn't work, but the project turned into a much deeper exploration of how home networks actually operate.

And perhaps that's the point of tinkering with hardware in the first place. Sometimes you set out to fix one annoying problem and end up learning an entirely different part of engineering.

Again, For the complete technical aspects, including the hardware investigation, UART access, bootloader exploration, firmware limitations, and the decisions that led to the final network architecture, read the original article: https://medium.com/@hiruthicsha/i-tried-to-hack-my-isp-router-it-turned-into-a-very-expensive-lesson-86cbdbba1fe7

Stay curious. Adios.
