articles.title: The Tests Are Green. Did the Agent Follow the Spec?
articles.description: When a coding agent writes the feature and the tests, a green test suite only tells you that its code...
articles.body_html:
When a coding agent writes the feature and the tests, a green test suite only tells you that its code agrees with its tests. Neither of those is your spec.

I wrote a guide to spec-driven development that covers how to write a spec for an agent and how to work with one in Claude Code, Spec Kit, OpenSpec and Kiro. Near the end I say the agent can still ignore the spec, so you still need tests and a review. This post picks up from there, with two checks that run in CI:

  1. A small script that proves every acceptance criterion has a test that really ran and passed.
  2. Mutation testing, which proves those tests fail when the code is wrong.

Everything below comes from a real run with Node 24, Vitest 5.0.5 and Stryker 10.1.1. You can copy the code as it is.

The setup: a small spec and a weak implementation

The spec is a shorter version of the CSV export example from the guide. The only thing I added is a stable ID on each criterion, so that a machine can follow it:

# Spec: Export transactions to CSV

## Acceptance criteria
- AC-1: WHEN the user exports with no filters
  THEN all their transactions are included, newest first.
- AC-2: WHEN a description contains a comma or quotes
  THEN the field is quoted and escaped (RFC 4180).
- AC-3: WHEN the filtered list is empty
  THEN the file has only the header row.

If you use Spec Kit, you already have IDs: its template numbers requirements as FR-001. You'd only change one regex in the script.

Then I wrote the code badly on purpose. It has a real bug, because escapeField handles commas and forgets about quotes:

// src/csv.js
const COLUMNS = ['date', 'description', 'category', 'account', 'amount']

function escapeField(value) {
  const text = String(value)
  if (text.includes(',')) return `"${text}"`
  return text
}

export function buildCsv(rows) {
  const sorted = [...rows].sort((a, b) => b.date.localeCompare(a.date))
  const lines = sorted.map((row) =>
    COLUMNS.map((column) => escapeField(row[column])).join(','),
  )
  return [COLUMNS.join(','), ...lines].join('\n')
}

The tests are weak on purpose too. Each one names its criterion in the title, and one of them is skipped. In the demo they sit inside a describe('buildCsv', ...) block, which is where the buildCsv > prefix in the reports below comes from:

// src/csv.test.js
import { expect, it } from 'vitest'
import { buildCsv } from './csv.js'

const row = (over = {}) => ({
  date: '2026-10-01',
  description: 'Coffee',
  category: 'Food',
  account: 'Checking',
  amount: 4.5,
  ...over,
})

it('AC-1: includes all transactions', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row(), row({ date: '2026-10-02' })])
  expect(csv.split('\n')).toHaveLength(3)
})

it('AC-2: escapes commas and quotes', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row({ description: 'Coffee, "large"' })])
  expect(csv).toContain('Coffee')
})

it.skip('AC-3: empty list gives only the header', () => {
  expect(buildCsv([])).toBe('date,description,category,account,amount')
})

Vitest is happy with this:

Tests  2 passed | 1 skipped (3)

A grep for the IDs is happy as well, since all three appear in the test file.

Check 1: does each criterion have a test that ran and passed?

The usual way to link specs to tests is to search the test files for the IDs. That search can't see .skip, so it would miss AC-3 here. The test runner knows what happened, so I read its report.

Have Vitest write JUnit XML:

// vitest.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config'

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    reporters: ['default', 'junit'],
    outputFile: { junit: 'reports/junit.xml' },
  },
})

Then compare the report with the spec:

// scripts/check-spec.mjs
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'

const [specPath = 'SPEC.md', junitPath = 'reports/junit.xml'] =
  process.argv.slice(2)
const ID = /\bAC-\d+\b/g

const specIds = new Set(readFileSync(specPath, 'utf8').match(ID) ?? [])

// id -> list of test outcomes: 'passed', 'failed' or 'skipped'
const results = new Map()
const junit = readFileSync(junitPath, 'utf8')
const testcases = junit.matchAll(
  /<testcase\b([^>]*?)(\/>|>([\s\S]*?)<\/testcase>)/g,
)

for (const [, attrs, , body = ''] of testcases) {
  const name = attrs.match(/\bname="([^"]*)"/)?.[1] ?? ''
  const outcome = body.includes('<skipped')
    ? 'skipped'
    : /<(failure|error)\b/.test(body)
      ? 'failed'
      : 'passed'

  for (const id of name.match(ID) ?? []) {
    results.set(id, [...(results.get(id) ?? []), outcome])
  }
}

const problems = []

for (const id of specIds) {
  const outcomes = results.get(id) ?? []
  if (outcomes.length === 0) problems.push(`${id}: no test`)
  else if (outcomes.includes('failed')) problems.push(`${id}: failing`)
  else if (!outcomes.includes('passed')) problems.push(`${id}: only skipped tests`)
}

for (const id of results.keys()) {
  if (!specIds.has(id)) problems.push(`${id}: test exists, not in spec`)
}

if (problems.length > 0) {
  console.error(`Spec check failed:\n  ${problems.join('\n  ')}`)
  process.exit(1)
}

console.log(`Spec check passed: ${specIds.size} criteria covered.`)

Run it against the code above:

$ node scripts/check-spec.mjs
Spec check failed:
  AC-3: only skipped tests

The last loop runs in the other direction and catches drift. When I renamed AC-3 to AC-4 in the spec, leaving the tests alone, both sides were reported:

Spec check failed:
  AC-4: no test
  AC-3: test exists, not in spec

The same script also worked unchanged on the JUnit output of Node's built-in runner (node --test --test-reporter=junit). Jest and Playwright can write JUnit too, but I didn't test those, so check how they mark skipped tests.

I removed the .skip, and the script went green:

Tests  3 passed (3)
Spec check passed: 3 criteria covered.

The feature is still wrong, though. The code doesn't escape quotes, and nothing tests the sort order. This script can only tell you that a test exists and passes. It has no idea whether expect(csv).toContain('Coffee') proves anything.

Check 2: would the tests notice if the code were wrong?

Mutation testing changes your code in small ways (it flips a condition, removes a method call, empties a string) and runs the tests against each changed version, called a mutant. If the tests still pass, the mutant survived, and that line of code isn't really being tested.

This is the question to ask about tests written by an agent, and you don't have to read them all to get an answer. Install Stryker:

npm i -D @stryker-mutator/core @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner

Add a config:

{
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "mutate": ["src/csv.js"],
  "reporters": ["clear-text", "progress"],
  "coverageAnalysis": "perTest"
}

Then npx stryker run. It took 3 seconds on this one file and found 6 survivors out of 21 mutants, for a score of 71.43%. These two are the interesting ones:

[Survived] ConditionalExpression
src/csv.js:5:7
-     if (text.includes(',')) return `"${text}"`
+     if (false) return `"${text}"`
Tests ran:
    buildCsv > AC-1: includes all transactions
    buildCsv > AC-2: escapes commas and quotes

[Survived] MethodExpression
src/csv.js:10:18
-     const sorted = [...rows].sort((a, b) => b.date.localeCompare(a.date))
+     const sorted = [...rows]
Tests ran:
    buildCsv > AC-1: includes all transactions
    buildCsv > AC-2: escapes commas and quotes
    buildCsv > AC-3: empty list gives only the header

The first mutant turns off the escaping entirely, and the AC-2 test still passes. The second deletes the sort, and the AC-1 test still passes. Those are the two features the spec asked for, and because the tests are named after criteria, the report points straight at the criteria with fake coverage.

Fixing what the mutants found

No mutant mentions the quotes bug. Stryker changes the code that exists, and the quote handling was never written. The mutant on line 5 only tells you the AC-2 test is too weak, and you find the bug when you fix the test:

const HEADER = 'date,description,category,account,amount'

it('AC-1: includes all transactions, newest first', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([
    row({ date: '2026-10-01' }),
    row({ date: '2026-10-03' }),
    row({ date: '2026-10-02' }),
  ])
  expect(csv.split('\n')).toEqual([
    HEADER,
    '2026-10-03,Coffee,Food,Checking,4.5',
    '2026-10-02,Coffee,Food,Checking,4.5',
    '2026-10-01,Coffee,Food,Checking,4.5',
  ])
})

it('AC-2: quotes fields with commas', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row({ description: 'Coffee, large' })])
  expect(csv).toContain(',"Coffee, large",')
})

it('AC-2: escapes quotes by doubling them', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row({ description: 'The "large" one' })])
  expect(csv).toContain(',"The ""large"" one",')
})

it('AC-3: empty list gives only the header', () => {
  expect(buildCsv([])).toBe(HEADER)
})

Now the bug shows up:

FAIL  src/csv.test.js > buildCsv > AC-2: escapes quotes by doubling them
Tests  1 failed | 3 passed (4)

Spec check failed:
  AC-2: failing

The fix is one line:

if (/[",]/.test(text)) return `"${text.replaceAll('"', '""')}"`

After that, the spec check passes and Stryker kills all 23 mutants, for a score of 100%. Don't expect that number on real code. This is one small function, and some mutants in a real project can't be killed because they don't change the behavior at all.

Running both in CI

The order matters: the tests write the report, the script reads it, and Stryker runs last because it's the slowest step.

- run: npx vitest run
- run: node scripts/check-spec.mjs
- run: npx stryker run

To make Stryker fail the build, add a threshold to its config. I checked this with a score of 95.65% against a break of 100, and it exits with code 1:

"thresholds": { "break": 80 }

The 80 is a starting point I picked for this post, so adjust it to what your codebase can hold. On a large project, point mutate at the files in the spec's "Files and interfaces" section, and use npx stryker run --incremental, which saves its results to a file and reuses them on the next run.

You can also give the survivors to the agent. Use a fresh session, and make it clear what it can't touch, because deleting the assertion or editing the spec is the fastest way to turn a check green:

These mutants survived Stryker. For each one, find the acceptance
criterion in SPEC.md that should have caught it, and strengthen that
test. Do not edit src/ or SPEC.md. If a stronger test fails because the
code is wrong, stop and tell me which criterion the code doesn't meet.

With Claude Code, you can run the same checks in a Stop hook. A hook blocks only on exit code 2 and the script exits with 1, so the hook command needs to convert it: npx vitest run; node scripts/check-spec.mjs || exit 2. I didn't run this hook in the demo.

What these checks can't tell you

Both checks work from the IDs in the test titles, and nothing verifies that a test labeled AC-2 is about AC-2. A strong test with the wrong label passes both. You still have to read the tests for the criteria that matter most, but the report tells you where to start.

The spec itself can also be wrong or incomplete. If nobody wrote the criterion for 100,000 rows, no script will ask about it. That part happens earlier, when you write and review the spec, and the guide has a full example, the agent interview prompt, and a comparison of Spec Kit, OpenSpec and Kiro.

I've only run this on a small example, so if you've used a mutation score as a CI check on code written by an agent, I'd like to know what threshold held up on a real codebase.

articles.title: How to Reverse Engineer a Web3 Frontend to Find Hidden API Endpoints
articles.description: How to Reverse Engineer a Web3 Frontend to Find Hidden API Endpoints   When we interact with...
articles.body_html:
How to Reverse Engineer a Web3 Frontend to Find Hidden API Endpoints

When we interact with Web3 applications—wallets, decentralized exchanges, or NFT marketplaces—we often assume everything is happening on the blockchain. But here is the reality: the blockchain is slow and expensive.

To provide a seamless user experience, most Web3 applications rely on centralized backend APIs. These APIs handle everything from fetching token prices and calculating fees to managing user profiles and transaction histories.

Because the frontend is usually built with modern frameworks like React or Next.js, this logic is hidden inside minified JavaScript bundles. Developers sometimes assume that because the code is hard to read, the API is secure.

In this article, I’m going to walk you through the methodology of reverse-engineering a Web3 frontend to find its hidden API, and how this process often leads to the discovery of unauthenticated endpoints.

The Illusion of the Frontend

When you visit a Web3 application, your browser downloads a massive bundle of JavaScript. This code is responsible for rendering the UI, connecting to your crypto wallet (like MetaMask), and communicating with the backend.

The first step in our journey is realizing that the frontend is a map to the backend.

If you open your browser's Developer Tools and look at the Network tab, you’ll see a flurry of requests. However, filtering through the noise can be exhausting. A more efficient approach is to pull the JavaScript bundles directly and analyze the source code.

Finding the Hidden Gateway

Once we extract the JavaScript files, we aren't looking for UI logic. We are looking for strings. Specifically, we are looking for hardcoded URLs.

Developers often hardcode their API gateways directly into the frontend code. During our recon, by extracting and searching through the frontend bundles, we found a specific API gateway (let's call it api.web3wallet.com/v2).

Once you have the base API URL, the game completely changes. You no longer need to click around the web app; you can talk directly to the server.

Mapping the Endpoints

With the API gateway in hand, the next step is to discover the routes. Web3 apps have predictable naming conventions. If the frontend shows a "Wallet" page, there is almost certainly an endpoint like /wallet/balance or /user/transactions.

By analyzing how the frontend JavaScript calls the API, we can map out the entire backend architecture. During our investigation, we found routes for:

  • User profiles
  • Token listings
  • Gas fee calculations
  • Transaction values

The Broken Access Control (BAC) Discovery

Here is where the vulnerability usually hides.

When an API endpoint is called, it should always verify who is making the request. This is done using an Authorization header, usually containing a Bearer Token (a JWT).

During our testing, we sent requests to several endpoints. Some correctly returned a 401 Unauthorized, proving that the backend was checking for a valid session.

However, we found an endpoint designed to list all available tokens in the ecosystem. When we sent a simple GET request without any tokens, cookies, or authorization headers, the server responded with 200 OK.

Not only was it accessible, but it returned a massive payload—nearly 500 Kilobytes of JSON data.

Why Information Disclosure Matters

Some developers might look at a leaked JSON file and think, "It's just a list of tokens, what's the harm?"

But looking closely at the data, we found:

  • Internal Testnet Addresses: Smart contract addresses used for testing, which could be targeted for testnet-specific exploits.
  • Hidden Tokens: Assets explicitly marked with "hide": true in the JSON, meaning they shouldn't be visible to the public.
  • Business Logic: Internal fee structures, transfer limits, and rate limits based on KYC tiers.

In the hands of an attacker, this data is gold. It allows them to map the internal infrastructure, understand the platform's logic, and find other vulnerabilities.

The Lesson for Developers

The biggest takeaway from this methodology is simple: Never trust the client.

  1. Secure Your APIs: Just because an endpoint is buried in minified React code does not mean it is private. If an endpoint shouldn't be public, enforce authentication and authorization on the backend.
  2. Minimize Data Exposure: Don't send your entire database schema to the frontend. Only send the specific data the user needs to see. Remove hidden tokens, internal testnet addresses, and sensitive configuration data from public API responses.
  3. Audit Your Frontend: Regularly review your JavaScript bundles to ensure you aren't leaking API keys, admin routes, or sensitive gateway information.

Reverse-engineering a Web3 frontend isn't about being a wizard; it's about understanding how the pieces connect. By following the trail of JavaScript, you can often find the hidden doors that developers forgot to lock.

articles.title: How we compress a PDF to an exact size in the browser, with no upload
articles.description: We are Mirza Games, a small independent studio in Dubai (on Google Play we publish as Sezarr). Most...
articles.body_html:
We are Mirza Games, a small independent studio in Dubai (on Google Play we publish as Sezarr). Most of what we build is puzzle games, but one of the most used things on our site is a plain PDF tool: compress a PDF to a size in KB. This post explains how it works, with excerpts from the real code.

The problem: "upload a PDF under 200 KB"

Job portals, exam sites and government forms love hard limits. "Certificate, PDF, max 200 KB." "Scanned ID, under 100 KB." The person filling in the form has one number in mind, and the file either passes or it does not.

Most compressors offer three buttons: low, medium, high. You pick one, check the size, and try again. If "high" gives 230 KB, there is no button for "a bit more". If it gives 40 KB, the scan may be unreadable, and the reviewer rejects it anyway.

So we set ourselves two goals:

  1. The user types a target (50, 100, 200, 300, 500 KB, 1 MB, or a custom number), and the file comes out at or under it.
  2. The output must stay readable. If the target is too small for that, we say so instead of returning mush.

Design choice: everything runs in the browser

The files people send to these portals are ID cards, mark sheets, bank letters. We did not want them on our server, so there is no server step at all. The page loads a small UI, and the heavy libraries load only when the user picks a file:

  • qpdf, compiled to WebAssembly (from @mssio/qpdf-wasm), running in its own Web Worker.
  • pdf-lib, for reading and rewriting PDF objects, also in a worker.
  • pdf.js (the legacy build, so older Android Chrome versions work) for rendering pages to a canvas.

All three are vendored in the repo, not loaded from a CDN. Our browser test fails if the page makes any request other than a same-origin GET (plus the analytics script and its hits), so "no upload" is checked on every run, not just promised.

The trade-off is that the user's device does all the work. A phone with 2 GB of RAM cannot hold a 300 dpi render of a large page, so the renderer caps each page canvas by navigator.deviceMemory: 1.6 megapixels on 2 GB devices, 2.6 on 4 GB, 4.2 above that. A very large page may then render below the dpi we want, and long documents simply take longer. The UI accepts files up to 300 MB, but big files are slow on weak devices. That is the cost of not uploading.

Three steps, stopping as soon as the target fits

The engine (compress.js) tries three steps in order, from least to most destructive. It returns the first result that is at or under the target.

Step 1: lossless repack

First we try to shrink the file without changing a single pixel or glyph. Two things run in parallel: qpdf with object streams, Flate recompressed at level 9 (--recompress-flate --compression-level=9, which also re-encodes some older filters), unused resources and the XMP metadata stream removed; and a plain pdf-lib re-save. The smaller one wins.

// 1. lossless
let base = { bytes: orig, size: orig.length };
const tries = await Promise.allSettled([qpdfOptimize(orig.slice()), run('resave', [orig.slice()])]);
for (const t of tries) if (t.status === 'fulfilled' && t.value.length < base.size) base = { bytes: t.value, size: t.value.length };
check();
if (base.size <= target) return { bytes: base.bytes, size: base.size, step: 'lossless', floor: false };
const candidates = [{ bytes: base.bytes, size: base.size, step: 'lossless' }]; // legible results, for the floor case

Promise.allSettled matters: if one tool chokes on a strange file, the other can still win. Note the candidates list too. Every readable result is kept, because we may need the smallest of them later.

Step 2: re-encode only the embedded images

If the file is still too big, the weight is almost always in images: a phone photo of a certificate, or a scan saved at 600 dpi. Step 2 touches only those images. Text, fonts and vector drawings stay exactly as they were.

pdf-lib lists the image objects we can safely rewrite: 8-bit RGB or grey, JPEG or Flate (with PNG predictors undone in the browser), and no masks or Decode arrays. Anything unusual is left alone.

For each image we need to know how big it is actually drawn on the page. A 4000-pixel-wide photo shown 3 inches wide does not need 4000 pixels. We walk pdf.js operator lists, track the transform matrix, and record the largest size each image is painted at. Then each image is offered at a few (dpi, JPEG quality) options:

export const IMAGE_OPTS = [[200, 0.82], [150, 0.82], [150, 0.68], [120, 0.78], [120, 0.65], [150, 0.55], [120, 0.5]];
// photographs (not scans of text) may go a little lower: no text to keep readable inside them
export const PHOTO_IMAGE_OPTS = [[100, 0.6], [100, 0.5]];
// scans of text stay sharp as JPEG only at >= 150 dpi, quality 0.7; below that, step 3's crisp 1-bit pages win
export const TEXT_IMAGE_OPTS = [[200, 0.82], [150, 0.82], [150, 0.7]];

A small probe of each image is classified as "text-like" (mostly white paper, very little colour) or not. Scanned text gets only the three conservative options; other images get the full list. Options larger than the original are dropped, and keeping the original is always allowed.

Picking one option per image so the total fits a budget is a small knapsack problem. We use a greedy chooser:

export function chooseOptions(sizes, budget) {
  const picks = sizes.map(() => 0);
  let total = sizes.reduce((a, s) => a + s[0], 0);
  while (total > budget) {
    let bi = -1, bs = -Infinity;
    for (let i = 0; i < sizes.length; i++) {
      const p = picks[i];
      if (p + 1 >= sizes[i].length) continue;
      const save = sizes[i][p] - sizes[i][p + 1];
      if (save > bs) { bs = save; bi = i; }
    }
    if (bi < 0) break;
    total += sizes[bi][picks[bi] + 1] - sizes[bi][picks[bi]];
    picks[bi]++;
  }
  // ... (if nothing fits, return the smallest option everywhere with fits: false)
  // fill: upgrade the cheapest steps while the budget allows

In words: start with the best option everywhere. While over budget, step down on whichever image saves the most bytes. Once it fits, go back and upgrade the cheapest steps while there is still room. That last pass is what gets the result close to the target instead of far under it.

The budget is the target minus the bytes that are not images, minus a rough 160 bytes of overhead per replaced image. The new JPEGs are swapped into the existing objects in place. Because our overhead guess can be off, the engine builds the real file, measures it, and if it is still over, shrinks the budget by the overshoot plus 512 bytes and tries again, up to four times.

Step 3: rasterise pages, only as a last resort

If text, fonts or vectors themselves are too heavy for the target, the only way down is to turn pages into images. This is the step that loses selectable text, so it runs last, and the result screen says plainly that the pages became images.

Each page is rendered with pdf.js at 150 dpi and classified with the same text-like test. Text pages are rendered again at 200 dpi and converted to 1-bit black and white: an Otsu threshold picks the ink/paper cut-off, pixels are packed eight to a byte, and the result is Flate-compressed with the browser's CompressionStream. A crisp 1-bit page is often much smaller than a blurry JPEG of the same page, and much easier to read. Text pages get 200, 150 and 120 dpi options.

Photo pages become JPEGs at 150 to 100 dpi, quality 0.8 down to 0.5, converted to greyscale if they had almost no colour anyway. The same chooseOptions picks one option per page:

let budget = target - (900 + 380 * n);
for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
  check();
  const ch = chooseOptions(pages.map((p) => p.opts.map((o) => o.size)), budget);
  const out = await buildR(ch.picks);
  const minDpi = Math.min(...pages.map((p, i) => p.opts[ch.picks[i]].dpi));
  if (out.length <= target) return { bytes: out, size: out.length, step: 'raster', kinds, floor: false, minDpi };
  if (!ch.fits) { candidates.push({ bytes: out, size: out.length, step: 'raster', kinds, minDpi }); break; }
  budget -= out.length - target + 512;
}
// Below the legibility floor: the smallest readable file we made.
const best = candidates.reduce((a, b) => (b.size < a.size ? b : a));
return { ...best, floor: true };

Floors: smallest readable size beats any size at all

Notice that every option list above ends somewhere. There is no "50 dpi, quality 0.2" option. The hard floors are:

  • text pages: 120 dpi, 1-bit
  • photo pages: 100 dpi, JPEG quality 0.5
  • embedded scans of text: 150 dpi, quality 0.7
  • other embedded images: 120 dpi, quality 0.5 (photographs 100 dpi)

If even the smallest options do not fit, the engine returns the smallest readable file it made in any step, flagged with floor: true. The UI then says "Smallest readable size is X" and names the download ..._smallest_readable.pdf.

We learned this the hard way: an earlier version always hit the number, and a text form compressed to 50 KB came out unreadable. Such a file is worse than useless. The portal accepts it, and the reviewer rejects the application later. An honest floor lets the user decide: ask for a higher limit, drop a page, or rescan.

How readability is tested. A headless Chrome test drives the real UI. It compresses five generated fixtures (a dense one-page form with an embedded font, a 5-page report, a 300 dpi scan, a photo brochure, a 20-page photo PDF) to 50, 100, 200 and 500 KB. A run passes only if:

  • the output is at or under the target, or the tool showed the floor message;
  • qpdf --check accepts the file;
  • the text stays legible. Original and output are both rendered with pdf.js at 150 dpi and compared only on text windows (small blocks where the original shows dark strokes on light paper). Mean SSIM must be at least 0.7, and edge sharpness (output relative to original) at least 0.75.

Those thresholds were calibrated against the old engine: its unreadable outputs scored 0.18 to 0.55 SSIM, while crisp results score 0.8 or more. Unit tests in Node cover the pure parts: chooseOptions (including the "nothing fits" case), the Otsu threshold and bit packing, image listing and replacement, and the 1-bit page builder, whose output qpdf must accept.

Units: what is a KB?

Portals disagree: some mean 1000 bytes, some 1024. We take the safer reading. A maximum KB is 1000 bytes, so a "200 KB" target means 200,000 bytes, which also passes a portal that allows 204,800. (Our photo tools also have minimum sizes; there a KB is 1024 bytes, for the same reason in reverse.) The result screen shows the exact byte count, so nobody has to guess.

What we learned, and the trade-offs

  • "Exact size" really means "at or under". The greedy fill gets close to the target, but we never pad a PDF upward. The point is passing the limit, not hitting it to the byte.
  • Order matters more than clever encoding. Steps 1 and 2 keep the text selectable. Rasterising is easy and tempting for everything; we kept it last on purpose.
  • We skip images we do not fully understand. Masks, Decode arrays and odd bit depths are left alone. Some files then need step 3, but none get a broken image.
  • Size estimates are guesses, so measure. Both the image and raster steps build the real file, check its length, and retry.
  • Client-side has real limits. Speed and render size depend on the device. We chose slow and private.
  • Readability needs a number. "Looks fine to me" did not catch the bad 50 KB form. A metric on text regions, with a threshold, did.

Try it

The tool is live at mirzagames.com/pdf/compress-pdf-to-kb/, and the other PDF tools (merge, split, photo to KB and more) are at mirzagames.com/pdf/. It runs fully in your browser, so you can test it on a real document. If you find a PDF that comes out unreadable, or that should have reached a target and did not, we would like to hear about it in the comments.

articles.title: Building hldays #7: Religious and cultural observances
articles.description: A public holiday is a legal fact: the law says the office is closed. A religious observance is...
articles.body_html:
A public holiday is a legal fact: the law says the office is closed. A religious observance is something else. Ramadan, Passover or Lunar New Year don't close anything in Lisbon, but a lot of people still plan around them: shift rotas, delivery windows, a marketing calendar, a meeting you shouldn't put on Yom Kippur.

So hldays has a second layer next to holidays: observances. There are 46 of them across six traditions (Western Christian, Orthodox Christian, Jewish, Islamic, Chinese and Buddhist), served by /v1/observances and attached to the date endpoints on paid plans.

I added them for exactly that kind of scheduling. The API already knew when offices close, and it felt incomplete not to know when a lot of people are busy anyway.

This post is mostly about the calendars, because that's where the interesting problems were.

Data first

Each tradition is one YAML file in data/observances/. An observance looks a lot like a holiday rule, with three extra ideas: a span (days or an end rule), an evening start (eve), and whether the date is a calculation that might be off (estimated):

- id: passover
  name: { en: "Passover", he: "פסח" }
  rule: { calendar_date: { calendar: hebrew, month: Nisan, day: 15 } }
  days: 8
  eve: true
  notes: "8 days in the diaspora, 7 in Israel."

The rule kinds are the same ones the holiday engine uses (src/core/dates.ts), so an observance can be a fixed date, an offset from Easter, an offset from Orthodox Easter, or a day in another calendar.

Easter: the one with an algorithm

Western Easter is the anonymous Gregorian algorithm, straight from the textbook:

/** Gregorian Easter Sunday (anonymous Gregorian algorithm). */
export function easterSunday(year: number): Date {
  const a = year % 19;
  const b = Math.floor(year / 100);
  const c = year % 100;
  // ... eleven more lines of integer arithmetic
  const month = Math.floor((h + l - 7 * m + 114) / 31);
  const day = ((h + l - 7 * m + 114) % 31) + 1;
  return new Date(Date.UTC(year, month - 1, day));
}

Everything movable in the Western calendar is an offset from it: Ash Wednesday is { easter: -46 }, Pentecost { easter: 49 }. The same function already drives holidays like Good Friday and Corpus Christi in the national data, so observances got it for free.

Orthodox Easter: same idea, different calendar

Orthodox churches compute Easter on the Julian calendar. The code uses Meeus' Julian algorithm and then shifts the result onto the Gregorian calendar:

/** Orthodox Easter Sunday as a Gregorian date (Meeus' Julian algorithm + Julian→Gregorian shift; valid 1900–2099). */
export function orthodoxEasterSunday(year: number): Date {
  const a = year % 4;
  const b = year % 7;
  const c = year % 19;
  const d = (19 * c + 15) % 30;
  const e = (2 * a + 4 * b - d + 34) % 7;
  const month = Math.floor((d + e + 114) / 31);
  const day = ((d + e + 114) % 31) + 1;
  const shift = Math.floor(year / 100) - Math.floor(year / 400) - 2; // 13 days in 1900–2099
  return addDays(new Date(Date.UTC(year, month - 1, day)), shift);
}

The shift line is the bit worth noticing: the gap between the two calendars grows by a day in most century years, and it's 13 days for the whole range hldays supports (2016 to 2099). The test includes the year both Easters coincide, which is a good sanity check:

expect(formatDate(orthodoxEasterSunday(2025))).toBe("2025-04-20"); // same day as Western Easter
expect(formatDate(orthodoxEasterSunday(2026))).toBe("2026-04-12");
expect(expandRule({ orthodox_easter: -48 }, 2026)).toEqual(["2026-02-23"]); // Greek Clean Monday

The YAML also notes a split inside Orthodoxy: Julian-calendar churches celebrate Christmas on 7 January, while Revised Julian churches (Greek, Romanian, Bulgarian) use 25 December but share the Orthodox Easter cycle. That's a note on the record, not two records.

Hebrew and Islamic dates: let Intl do it

I didn't want to ship conversion tables for every calendar. JavaScript's Intl.DateTimeFormat already knows the Hebrew and Islamic calendars (through ICU), so the engine builds an index for a Gregorian year by formatting every day of it:

fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat(`en-u-ca-${calendar}`, { timeZone: "UTC", month: "numeric", day: "numeric" });
// Intl silently falls back to Gregorian when a runtime lacks the calendar; wrong dates are worse than an error.
if (fmt.resolvedOptions().calendar !== calendar) throw new Error(`Intl calendar ${calendar} is not supported`);

That second line is my favourite in the file. If a runtime doesn't support a calendar, Intl doesn't throw: it quietly formats Gregorian dates instead. Without the check, a runtime without full ICU would treat Islamic month 10, day 1 as 1 October and put Eid al-Fitr there. I checked that the output on Cloudflare Workers matches Node before relying on it.

The Hebrew calendar had one naming trap. In leap years there are two Adars, and Intl calls the second one "Adar II". Purim is in Adar II in leap years, so the index stores "Adar II" under "Adar":

const month = parts.find((p) => p.type === "month")!.value.replace(/^Adar II$/, "Adar");


// "Adar" is Adar II in leap years (Purim)
expect(expandRule(purim, 2024)).toEqual(["2024-03-24"]);
expect(expandRule(purim, 2025)).toEqual(["2025-03-14"]);

Islamic dates are estimates, and the API says so

The Islamic calendar is lunar, and in many countries a month starts when the new moon is actually sighted. No algorithm can know that in advance. hldays calculates with the Umm al-Qura calendar (Saudi Arabia's), and the YAML says up front what that means:

# Islamic observances, calculated with the Umm al-Qura calendar (Saudi Arabia). Many countries start months on
# a local moon sighting, so the observed date can differ by a day: every entry is marked estimated.

Every Islamic observance has estimated: true, and it comes through in the response so clients can show "around" instead of a firm date. Here's Eid al-Fitr on a business-day call (paid plan, run locally):

{
  "jurisdiction": { "id": "PT-M-1106", "name": "Lisboa", ... },
  "date": "2026-03-20",
  "business_day": true,
  "holidays": [],
  "observances": [
    { "observance_id": "eid-al-fitr", "tradition": "islamic", "name": { "en": "Eid al-Fitr", "ar": "عيد الفطر" },
      "start": "2026-03-20", "end": "2026-03-22", "starts_previous_evening": true, "estimated": true }
  ]
}

starts_previous_evening comes from eve: true: Jewish and Islamic days begin at sunset, so Eid "on" 20 March starts on the evening of the 19th.

A lunar year is about 11 days shorter than a Gregorian one, which breaks a quiet assumption: that a date happens once a year. Eid al-Fitr happens twice in 2033. The rule expander returns a list for that reason, and the test makes it explicit:

// The Islamic year is ~11 days shorter, so some Gregorian years hold the same date twice
expect(expandRule(eid, 2033)).toHaveLength(2);

Spans that cross New Year

Ramadan doesn't have a fixed length: it's 29 or 30 days. So instead of days, it has an end rule: the day before 1 Shawwal.

- id: ramadan
  rule: { calendar_date: { calendar: islamic-umalqura, month: 9, day: 1 } }
  end: { calendar_date: { calendar: islamic-umalqura, month: 10, day: 1, offset: -1 } }

Around 2030 Ramadan starts in December and ends in January. Asking "what's observed on 5 January 2031?" has to find a span that started the previous year, so Observances.between always looks one year back:

// A span can start in the previous Gregorian year (Ramadan across New Year).
for (let y = Number(from.slice(0, 4)) - 1; y <= Number(to.slice(0, 4)); y++) {


{ "date": "2031-01-05", "data": [{ "observance_id": "ramadan", "start": "2030-12-26", "end": "2031-01-23", "estimated": true, ... }] }

The Chinese calendar: where Intl was wrong

I started with Intl for the Chinese calendar too. Then I compared it with the Hong Kong Observatory's published tables and found that ICU gets 5 of the 1039 month starts between 2016 and 2099 wrong by a day. Two of them are Chinese New Year: 2027 and 2030.

You can see it in Node (ICU 78.3):

2027-02-06 12/30 <- ICU: last day of the 12th month
2027-02-07 1/1 <- ICU: New Year
2030-02-02 1/1 <- ICU: New Year

The HKO tables say 6 February 2027 and 3 February 2030. Being a day off on the biggest date in the calendar wasn't acceptable, so for the Chinese calendar only, hldays uses HKO's data. scripts/import-chinese-calendar.ts downloads one text file per year and keeps just the month starts:

const m = /^(\d{4})\/(\d{1,2})\/(\d{1,2})\s+(\d{1,2})(?:st|nd|rd|th) Lunar Month/.exec(line);
if (!m) continue;
const month = Number(m[4]);
// HKO repeats the month number for a leap month
const leap = month === prevMonth;
starts.push(`${m[1]}-${m[2].padStart(2, "0")}-${m[3].padStart(2, "0")} ${month}${leap ? "L" : ""}`);

The result is src/core/chinese-months.json: 1077 entries like "2014-01-31 1", from 2014 to 2100. Leap months are marked L and never match a rule, so "2nd month, day 1" in 2023 is the regular second month and not the leap one that follows it. The tests check the exact days ICU gets wrong:

// 2027 and 2030 are days ICU's Chinese calendar gets wrong; the engine uses the HKO table
expect([2025, 2026, 2027, 2030].flatMap((y) => expandRule(lny, y))).toEqual(["2025-01-29", "2026-02-17", "2027-02-06", "2030-02-03"]);

The table starts in 2014, not 2016, and git history explains why. The first version guarded the range strictly and rejected 2014, but /v1/observances?year=2016 needs it: observances always look one year back (for spans like Ramadan), and Lunar New Year's Eve is "1st month, day 1, offset -1", where an offset makes the engine expand the neighbouring years too. 2016 reaches 2015, and 2015 reaches 2014. A test now asks for the first and last day of the supported range, so that can't come back.

Observances never affect business days

This was a design rule from the first commit of the feature: observances are information, not days off. The business-day code doesn't read them at all. isBusinessDay looks at the weekend and at holidays, and observances are attached to the response afterwards:

const result = calendar.isBusinessDay(j, d, types(c), municipal);
return c.json({
  jurisdiction: summary(j),
  date: d,
  ...result,
  holidays: withSources(c)(result.holidays),
  ...observancesOn(c, d),
  ...
});

Where an observance is a day off, like Good Friday in Portugal, it's also a holiday in that country's data, with a source. The observance list just tells you it's Good Friday; the holiday list tells you the office is closed. Mixing the two would mean Eid closes Lisbon, which it doesn't.

Plans and limits

Observances are on the paid plans only. On the free plan, /v1/observances returns 403 paid_plan_required, and the date endpoints return observances: [] with an observances_notice that says how many were hidden, so a free client still knows something is there.

What isn't covered yet:

  • Theravada Vesak. The Buddhist file has only the East Asian Buddha's Birthday; Vesak needs a lunar calendar the engine doesn't support.
  • Hindu and Sikh calendars. Nothing yet.
  • Regional variants. Jewish festivals use diaspora lengths (Israel's are in notes), Shia dates for Mawlid are a note, and Korea and Vietnam can differ from China by a day where their time zone does.

Which calendar would you want next: Hindu, Vesak, or something else? Tell me in the comments.

Next in the series: making an API agent-friendly with MCP, and designing tools for Claude and other agents.
